What they said...

"In the strictest metal tradition, many tracks are just frenzied riffs with Roth rapping on top. And surprisingly enough, there's nothing here as slick as the two singles on Van Halen's post-Roth LP. Luckily, Vai's guitar work provides a rough enough roller-coaster ride to counter the lack of more melodic hooks." (

Rolling Stone

)

"With everybody from Patti to Belinda to Peter to Eldra kissing pop's ass, Roth gives it a pinch and keeps on trucking. Maybe because he lived out his wimpier fantasies on last year's EP, here he's free to mastermind his own piece of multiplatinum potential. Sure he covers

That's Life

, but he also assembles a metal band that'll cut old buddies: Maynard Ferguson drummer, cult heaven bassist, and on guitar former Zappa and Lydon sideman Steve Vai, who splits the difference between parody and virtuosity." (

Robert Christgau

)

"The "diamond" one set out to out-Van Halen Van Halen with his band's first effort,

Eat 'Em and Smile

, a more than adequate substitute for the overtly commercial tendencies of the "new and improved" original. Why mess with a winning recipe, indeed. Guitarist Steve Vai, bassist Billy Sheehan, and drummer Gregg Bissonette sound perfectly at home aping their boss's old cronies on such sizzling party anthems as

Shyboy

and

Elephant Gun.

" (

AllMusic

)

What you said...

Nick Tedds:

I remember thinking at the time of release that

Eat ‘Em And Smile

was an excellent album in parts. Lead single

Yankee Rose

is innovative/gimmicky enough to stand out from the crowd,

Shyboy

an opportunity for the Vai/Sheehan combo to showcase their twiddly histrionics, and

Ladies Nite in Buffalo

has a huge funky groove that is different but works well alongside the aforementioned opening tracks.

Goin’ Crazy

is also catchy enough.

After that though... I’m not a fan of the lounge-swing approach of

I’m Easy,

and

That’s Life

. The cover of

Tobacco Road

is fairly pointless, and

Bump And Grind

offers nothing new at all. It’s not often that I think an album of just over half an hour in length may have been better if it had been trimmed a little! But then again, that’s exactly what I thought about Roth’s last effort with Van Halen,

1984,

although, as with that album, the musicianship is undeniably of the highest quality and Ted Templeman’s production is top-notch.

Adam Ranger

: Controversial opinion: Diamond Dave is not as good as he thinks he is. The first three Van Halen albums were great, a sum of their parts rather than just one individual.

But I find this a bit one-dimensional and uninspiring. Great musicians on it, no question. But Dave having "fun" does not mean a good record. No song on this album stands out, and I would be quite happy not to hear it again.

Mark Herrington

: Mixed feelings about this one. There are some good tracks and great guitar pyrotechnics throughout. However, the sheer amount of covers at the expense of original material, and the weaker second half, drains some of that initial enthusiasm.

I love the punchy party rock on

Yankee Rose

, a great track and a great start, the standout track by miles here.

Shyboy

is a good display of guitar pyrotechnics, although not as catchy as

Yankee Rose.

The bluesy cover

I’m Easy

is a bit Dad Rock, but the guitar is great.

Ladies Night

lacks oomph, with good guitar.

Goin' Crazy

is a return to energetic party rock, with a weakish chorus rescued by great guitar.

Tobacco Road

– another cover – ushers in the weaker second half, and it's better than anything that follows. The tracks are just average from here, and finish with another cover in

That's Life

.

Some good stuff, some great guitar, but the album is short on ideas and consistency. If anything, it just gets me reaching for my copy of

Van Halen I

, to hear it done properly.

Chris Elliott

: In simple terms, it sounds like Van Halen. So that pretty much tells you if you'll like it. It's harmless FM rock that passes by without annoying or engaging. At my age, I don't think I'm about to be converted

Chris Downie

: Given the endlessly-publicised fallout over the split in the Van Halen camp in 1985, it was inevitable that both David Lee Roth's full-length debut and the first 'Van Hagar' effort

5150

would be intertwined with one another, far too often compared directly, as opposed to being viewed as distinct entities in their own right and enjoyed (or otherwise) on their own merits.

While the revamped Van Halen decided, at first, to continue the musical path taken on the mega-selling

1984

album (before paring back the keyboards on the provocatively titled follow-up

OU812

a few years later, and even more so on the heavier remaining 'Van Hagar' outings), Roth decided to go all-in with his cabaret clown show, albeit to mildly entertaining effect.

Where his solo career fell short, however, was in his failure to evolve beyond his first three solo efforts, culminating in the impressive

A Little Ain't Enough,

which was underpinned by the incredible talent of the young Jason Becker.

While the debut EP, replete with Beach Boys tribute, gave hints of what was to come, this full-length hits the spot when on point (

Yankee Rose

needs no introduction, but

Shyboy

is also impressive) but tails off in the second half. Moreover, its sparse running time of 31 minutes – two tracks of which are cover versions – treads the same path that held back the otherwise brilliant innovation of early Van Halen. Love it or hate it, the Van Hagar lineup evolved impressively and remained on top, while Roth's career stagnated and ultimately faded into a novelty act by the mid-90s.

Decades further down the line and taking a fresh perspective, if

Eat 'Em And Smile

does one thing in 2026, it tells us the original Van Halen line up were a product of their time, an exciting breath of fresh air that ushered in the American 80's metal scene two years before that decade even began, but which also burned out just as the second wave they heavily influenced, such as Dokken, Ratt, Twisted Sister et al, were hitting their peak. Despite their individual brilliance, they were somehow greater than the sum of their parts, but when divided, it was Roth who ultimately fell by the wayside, into self-parody. 7/10.

Gary Claydon

: Flawed but fun offering from the King of good-time metal. Neverthess,

Eat 'Em and Smile

is more hit than miss, thanks in large part to a genuinely killer band (ably aided and abetted by Ted Templeman's spot-on production), with Vai's guitar the real star of the show.

Raucous album opener, the classic

Yankee Rose

is a perfect illustration of Diamond Dave's technicolour, larger-than-life approach to rock'n'roll and the obvious stand-out track. The easy strut and groove of

Ladies' Night In Buffalo

runs it close, while

Big Trouble

has a lesser-spotted semi-serious DLR lyric. Elsewhere, there is plenty of energy, but a heavy whiff of filler lingers, and the covers are a waste of the talent on show.

Brian Carr:

A lot of memories for me on this one. I saw some great shows in my first three years of concert-going, and DLR on this tour was one of my favourites - his band were white hot! Steve Vai is in my top ten favourite guitar players; Billy Sheehan is almost certainly in my top five favourite bass players. The videos were loads of fun.

Ladies Night In Buffalo

was the second or third song I learned on bass. And, of course, I absolutely loved the

Eat 'Em And Smile

record.

Times and musical tastes change over the decades, though. I found and bought a used vinyl copy in recent years, but haven’t listened to it often. The album is still fun, and the performances are still electric. I still love Vai and Sheehan, and Bissonette is a fantastic drummer and perfect fit for the band. But listening 40 years later(!!!), it’s really hard to forget how poorly Dave’s schtick aged.

I’m Easy

and

That’s Life

may be fun, but on a record barely longer than 30 minutes, it screams padding and shows that Dave’s idea of entertainment is simultaneously inside

and

outside the norm. It’s also hard to ignore that

Eat ‘Em And Smile

was, in my opinion, the apex - it all went downhill from here. Five years later, I saw Roth again in what I will always remember as one of the worst concerts I’ve ever seen.

All of that said, it’s still great to hear Roth in his ADHD prime, together with one of the greatest rock lineups.

Philip Qvist

: It is a fun album, with great guitar pyrotechnics from Steve Vai backed by a solid rhythm section of Billy Sheehan and Gregg Bissonette, while Diamond Dave does what he does best, i.e. being Diamond Dave. None of the songs should be taken seriously, which was probably the real purpose of

Eat 'Em And Smile

, hence the cover versions.

There is nothing here that surprises me, and the songs are exactly what you expect from David Lee Roth, with song titles such as

Bump And Grind, Elephant Gun

and Ladies

Night in Buffalo

, with lyrics to match. The standout track is the opener,

Yankee Rose

(which I believe is a tribute to the Statue of Liberty).

So this is a fun and enjoyable album, but it's also a disposable one. The fact is that David Lee Roth needed Van Halen as much as Van Halen needed him (and this is not a slight against Sammy Hagar). No more than a 7 from me this week, but at least this album title inspired "Van Hagar" to name their next album

OU812

.

Mike Canoe

: I love it, I love it, and no one can change my mind.

Eat ‘Em And Smile

finds David Lee Roth trying to out Van Halen Van Halen by building his own perfect beast and I, for one, think, on this one album, that he succeeded, especially compared to the recently released

5150

and its emphasis on ballads and,

gasp

, pop songcraft.

Steve Vai made the lead guitar ridiculously

Hot For Teacher

fun again on songs like the giddy opener

Yankee Rose

and sex positive

Bump And Grind

. Fellow recruit Billy Sheehan was referred to in the music press at the time as the "Eddie Van Halen of bass." And while drummer Gregg Bissonette didn't have the name recognition of the rest of the band, he certainly knew what he was doing, whether on ravers like

Shyboy

or

Elephant Gun

or lounge lizards like

I'm Easy

or

That's Life

.

The band brings out the best in Roth. Roth was Van Halen's hype man (and he knew it), and he brings that same manic energy and showmanship here while still showing a (relative) maturity on

Ladies' Nite in Buffalo?

and

Big Trouble

. Interestingly, I used to hate

Goin' Crazy

because of those %$#@ing keyboards, but now it's one of my favourites.

Roth knew from the success of

Diver Down

that the majority of fans don't care if a song's a cover if it's "Van Halen'd" enough, and that's what he and his new band do with

Tobacco Road

. I don't think Roth ever got enough credit for his sense of humour or eclectic taste in cover choices. It's not like a hard rock band covering Frank Sinatra was a shoo-in for commercial success until Roth already proved it could be done with

Ain't Got Nobody/Just a Gigolo

.

Roth has been slagged since Van Halen's inception as a terrible singer, and I absolutely do not give a shit. He made rock'n'roll more fun than just about anybody before or since.

His prevailing fatal flaw has always been that he thinks he is the sole genius in the room instead of a vital part of a team. The ridiculously steep decline of his solo career indicates his need for talented collaborators. Roth had the ability to make already good things great. He thought he was coffee, but he was just the cream. (No,

you're

making it gross.)

Still, I would argue that

Eat 'Em and Smile

was the last great Van Halen album until 2012's

A Different Kind of Truth

. Roth, like the rest of Van Halen, was closely identified with the big, bright 1980s. It’s unlikely that a mid-’90s VH album with Roth would have fared much better than

Balance

or

VHIII

. Still, Roth may have been the fourth most musically talented member of any Van Halen lineup he was in, but he was always the most fun.

Marco Edwards:

Great album.

John Davidson

: We all loved Van Halen, but they never really topped their explosive debut, and while

1984

was a chart-bothering return to form, the writing was on the wall that DLR and the Van Halens were on different trajectories. Dave wanted pop hits, and with a couple of hit solo singles under his belt, he left the band to set out on his own.

It's ironic then that

Eat 'Em And Smile

sounds like a more natural follow-up to

1984

than

5150

. Though

5150

scuppered any hope EVH had of avoiding the charts with its AOR sound and the solid punch of Sammy Hagar.

It's not as if DLR had to downgrade the musicianship on his solo run either, though. Steve Vai brings the guitar chops that are every bit as good as Eddie's, Sheehan is arguably a better bassist than Michael Anthony, and Gregg Bissonette is no slouch on the drums either.

The two standouts are

Yankee Rose

and

Tobacco Road

, but songs like

Elephant Gun

rip along like the best early Van Halen, mixing guitar wig-outs and bass runs with the staccato drumming of

Hot For Teacher

.

I didn't pay this much heed at the time, but it brought a smile today, and at just over 30 minutes long, it doesn't hang around long enough to get tiresome. 8/10.

Mark Veitch

: I loved this album when I was in my teens, but then I also loved Skittles back then too! For such a great band, disappointing they could only come up with six new songs and padded out the album with covers.

Yankee Rose

and

Ladies Night In Buffalo

are the stand-out tracks, and live they were a top band, but this album doesn’t get many spins these days, and Dave's career quickly tailed off in line with his hairline and the 80s.

Adam Halpin

: Great music and awful lyrics.

David R. Howard

: This is a great record. I still listen to it.

Nigel Mawdsley

: I do like, and indeed own, some of Dave Lee Roth's solo albums but find

Eat 'Em And Smile

a little one-dimensional. There's no denying the superb musicianship and production, but I found the original songs very 'samey' and merging into one.

The cover of

Tobacco Road

seems to get stuck in a similar groove to the rest of the album; it's a great song, but I always feel there's something lacking when I play it.

Generally the album's okay, but Diamond Dave, as a solo artist, went on to produce better material. 6 out of 10.

Erik Schiavo

: This Buffoon's last shining moment. This tour was great.

Greg Schwepe

: So, still trying to figure this out.

Huge

Van Halen fan (of both eras) since day one. Love DLR and his sense of humor, swagger, attitude, and the overall concept of “Dave Being Dave.” But I did not rush out and buy this (or any other DLR solo albums) at the time it was released. It wasn’t until I had access to his entire catalogue via the streaming platforms that I actually listened to

Eat 'Em And Smile

in its entirety. But, at the time I liked everything I heard on the radio or saw on MTV. Probably more MTV.

Maybe I wasn’t too excited about him being backed by another group of musicians besides Eddie, Alex, and Mike? Which is silly, because, wow, did he enlist some musician firepower on this album or what? Or maybe I was staying loyal to Brand Van Halen even though one of the main ingredients had been swapped out and the recipe had changed. Or was it just that in some cases I have little interest in a solo album from someone even though they were a member of one of my favourite bands?

The first thing I noticed when listening again was the brevity of the album at 30 minutes. Get in, state your musical case, then get out.

This album runs the gamut from full-on, hard-rocking, guitar-fueled songs (

Yankee Rose, Goin’ Crazy, Elephant Gun

), a little jump blues (

I’m Easy

), and the show tune vibe of album closer

That’s Life

complete with strings and horns. All done DLR style. I tend to think Dave adheres to my own personal motto: “anything worth doing is worth overdoing.” So he’s all over the board here in those 30 minutes, but it’s all just enough and not too much. I must have listened to this 2-3 times today and have come to appreciate it more. Nothing “dark” here, just Dave bringing the

fun

.

And since this was released about four months after

5150

, you’re going to get the inevitable “well, which one was better?” discussions. And I say they’re too hard to compare, as the difference between them was way too far apart.

8 out of 10 on this one for me. “Dave Being Dave” is a good way to spend a half hour.

Mike Sargent:

The only DLR solo album that is worth a spin.

pending_news.title: Lamb Of God's Randy Blythe on doing what he does best
pending_news.rss_body:
Lamb Of God

frontman Randy Blythe admits he wouldn't describe himself as a "really good musician" – but he knows he's "really good at being in Lamb Of God."

The vocalist believes that never thinking of himself as the best at anything helps him to continue on a path of continual improvement, insisting that the moment you think of yourself as the best, "then you're shit."

Blythe tells Metal On Top: "I'm only good at one or two things, so I might as well just do what I'm good at.

I'm a pretty good writer and I'm a pretty good photographer. Not the best in the world. But I'm pretty good at being in Lamb of God.

"I'm not gonna say I'm a really good musician, but I'm really good at being in Lamb Of God."

He adds that when you think you are perfect, you lose the drive required to truly deliver.

"That's when your talent abandons you," he says. "When you become convinced of your own genius or whatever and that you can do no wrong, then you're not striving anymore.

"As an artist, whatever medium you're working in, in the moment of creation, you're struggling with yourself. You're trying to understand yourself and your place within the world. And in that moment, you're also trying to move beyond your own talent level.

"So, every time we make a record, I'm trying to do something I didn't think I could do before, not reinventing the wheel. And every time I write, I'm trying to write above my talent level, rather than just sitting in a sort of medium, because that's when you get lazy."

In the wide-ranging interview, Blythe also discusses his sparing use of clean vocals and how he avoids being affected by online negativity. View video of the full interview below.

Lamb Of God released their latest album

Into Oblivion

earlier this year.

pending_news.title: The wild 1970s glam rock classic inspired by The Beatles, Wagner… and Humphrey Bogart
pending_news.rss_body:
It took weeks to record, with an odd choice of producer and no record label involved. But it kick-started an iconic career. The album was 1972’s self-titled debut by

Roxy Music

, and it contained all the elements that would make them legendary. And for guitarist

Phil Manzanera

it was a hectic time. “I was only officially confirmed in the band on February 14, 1972, and a month later we were in the studio.”

Manzanera had auditioned the previous October, but lost out to former Nice man David O’List. But when the band played in front of EG Management in early February ’72, there was a fight between O’List and drummer Paul Thompson. As a result, EG took on the band but insisted on O’List going.

So in came Manzanera, joining Thompson, frontman Bryan Ferry, bassist Graham Simpson, synth player Brian Eno and saxophonist Andy Mackay. And, funded by EG, Roxy went to Command Studios in central London on March 14, working with producer Pete Sinfield, best known as the lyricist for

King Crimson

. “EG managed him, so they kept it in the family. I don’t why he was chosen, but the good thing is that Pete let us get on with it.”

Roxy recorded live in the studio, with few overdubs. But the band had rehearsed so much that they were ready to do it this way. “We were a band of inspired amateurs back then, who worked very hard and had lots of enthusiasm. And the album has a charm all of its own as a result.”

Roxy Music in 1972: (from left) Paul Thompson, Brian Ferry, Andy Mackay, Phil Manzanera, Brian Eno

(Image credit: Gijsbert Hanekroot/Redferns)

The songs were written by Ferry, bearing a number of cinematic references, something that delighted Manzanera. “That’s one of the things the two of us bonded over – we loved films. And to hear something like

2HB

, with its tribute to Humphrey Bogart, or

Chance Meeting

[inspired by the classic movie

Brief Encounter

] was just incredible. Bryan had so many ideas, and I always thought the rest of us provided the music for his words.”

The opening song,

Re-Make/Re-Model

, actually sums up the band’s eclecticism, with nods to

The Beatles

, Duane Eddy and… Wagner. “We all got the chance at the end to do our own thing. It’s a mad journey with lots of energy and it’s so exciting. It immediately says who we were – a band who would try anything."

While Roxy had a big hit with

Virginia Plain

later in 1972, reaching No.4 in the chart, this was recorded four months after the album and not included in the track listing. “In those days, we liked to keep singles separate and not feature them on albums.”

Apart from the music, what immediately stands out is the cover, featuring model Kari-Ann Muller. It set Roxy apart from almost everyone. “This cover was so striking that we’re going to be using it to promote our January UK tour – it still looks so good even now.”

The album was eventually released through Island, thanks to a licensing deal done by EG. “We got £5,000 from the label for a five-year lease. In those days, that was very innovative. I know EG had to fight to persuade some people at Island to put this out. But it did well for them.”

Roxy Music

reached No.10 in the UK charts, selling over 100,000 copies. As Manzanera concludes: “This was just the beginning. The rest is history.”

Originally published in Classic Rock issue 150 (March 2010)

pending_news.title: Mastodon announce Marrow Deep Bone Dust edition vinyl containing fragments of actual mastodon fossil
pending_news.rss_body:
Mastodon

are to release a very limited edition 2LP vinyl version of their latest album

Marrow Deep

– with fragments of actual mastodon fossil pressed into the records.

Only 170 of the double vinyl 'Bone Dust Edition' of Marrow Deep are being made available, due to the "finite quantity of bone dust available."

Fans are required to enter

a raffle through Loma Vista Recordings

for a chance to purchase one of the sets at a cost of $150.

They are only available for shipping to the USA, Canada and Mexico.

The idea was hatched by bassist Troy Sanders.

The band say: "About 20 years ago, we were given a giant bag of mastodon teeth. Not display-worthy fossils, but a collection of teeth that left us wondering what to do with them.

"Troy eventually had the wild idea to turn them into powder and press them directly into a vinyl record. Huge thanks to Loma Vista Recordings for connecting us with Waxworks to make this dream a reality."

The Bone Dust package also includes a certificate of authenticity.

Sanders adds: "How cool is it to juxtapose something with 11,000 year old fossils with a modern 2026 Mastodon record?"

The process of sprinkling the fossil dust into the vinyl wax before pressing was assisted by a geologist from the University of Georgia. A video detailing the work can be viewed below.

Marrow Deep

was released in August, following the departure and subsequent

death of founding guitarist Brent Hinds.

Metal Hammer's review of the record describes it as the band having "snatched joy from the jaws of heartbreak."

pending_news.title: Tuomas Holopainen reflects on 30 years of Nightwish
pending_news.rss_body:
On October 15, 2026 it was announced that Nightwish had

parted ways with vocalist Floor Jansen

after 13 years. In statements released by both Floor and the group, they described the split as "a mutual decision". At the time of writing, both parties and unavailable for comment.

Earlier this summer Hammer flew out to Finland to spend time with founder Tuomas Holopainen in the band's birthplace of Kitee to discuss 30 years of Nightwish history and what the future might look like.

On June 16, 2023,

Nightwish

played the best gig of their lives. That’s how founder and keyboardist

Tuomas Holopainen

sees it, anyway. Looking out at a sold-out crowd at Kitee’s Rantakenttä baseball stadium, he recognised more faces than usual – friends, cousins, siblings, fans who’d travelled across the world. This was the first time Nightwish had played in their hometown in almost 20 years and, for Tuomas, it felt like he’d come full circle.

“When we got onstage, I could almost see the studio building where we’d recorded our very first demo,” he says now. “I remembered being there almost 30 years before, now I’m playing to 11,000 people. I still get shivers just thinking about it. What a journey!”

Several songs from the Kitee gig appear on a new live compilation,

The Greatest 30 Years On Earth

, released in December to coincide with Nightwish’s 30th anniversary. Since forming in this small rural town in 1996, the band have risen to become their country’s biggest musical export and one of the defining groups of the 21st century, doing more than anyone to shape the modern

symphonic metal

movement.

Despite everything he’s achieved, Tuomas still lives here in Kitee. He isn’t just its most famous son, he’s its biggest cheerleader. So much so that he’s agreed to give

Hammer

a tour of his birthplace. It’s clear that Tuomas Holopainen loves Kitee. And Kitee loves Tuomas Holopainen back.

“What brings you here?” asks the taxi driver who collects us from the local train station. We’re here to write a piece about Nightwish, we explain.

“Ah, you’ll be seeing Tuomas then,” she says. “Tell him I said hello.”

“I know her,” Tuomas says with a chuckle, when we meet him for our tour the next day. “I mean, there’s, like, three taxi drivers out here. It’s a small town.”

To understand just how remarkable Nightwish’s rise has been, you first have to understand just how remote Kitee is. A four-hour-plus train ride away from Helsinki, civilisation drops away and we’re treated to the sights of Finland’s rugged wilderness. Trees. Trees. More trees. A lake. More trees.

There’s something about being on an island – you can’t just walk away

Tuomas Holopainen

With a population of fewer than 10,000 and one main road, Kitee is more like a glorified waystation than a town in the traditional sense. But Tuomas insists he’s never been tempted to up sticks for the bright lights of the big city.

“Never,” he says proudly. “I’ve always been a country boy. I just love this town because I know everybody and everybody knows me, so I get this peace and solitude. It’s a safe haven.”

It’s appropriate that he’s acting as our tour guide today. One of his first jobs as a teenager was showing people around the local Lutheran church. His grandfather served as pastor there before Tuomas was born, and the Nightwish man can trace his mother’s family line back to 16th-century religious reformist Martin Luther himself. The young Tuomas preferred fantasy novels and movies to scripture, and he still holds the fantastical close to his heart today. The otherwise unassuming car he picks us up in for our tour of the town is nicknamed ‘Gryffindor’. “The licence plate says ‘GRF’,” he says sheepishly, adding that there’s a large Harry Potter flag in the boot.

Encouraged into music by his mother, he learned piano and later played clarinet and the saxophone in his school’s classical and jazz groups. It was there that he met future Nightwish guitarist Emppu Vuorinen and singer Tarja Turunen. On July 6, 1996, when he was 19, Tuomas invited the pair to his parents’ cabin on an island in nearby Lake Pyhäjärvi to create a new band. Sitting around a campfire, he shared songs he’d written while doing his national service in the Finnish army. It was the moment Nightwish were born.

“In the guestbook, you can find the inscription saying that a band had formed that day,” Tuomas says. “It doesn’t say ‘Nightwish’, but it says we were there.”

He bought the island home from his parents a few years ago, and goes there a few times a year to write lyrics.

“There’s no electricity or running water, it’s very primal,” he says. “That’s why I like it. It’s very solitary and peaceful. There’s something about being on an island – you can’t just walk away.”

(Image credit: John McMurtrie)

Kitee was once the moonshine capital of Finland, famous for its illicit hooch. Today, one of its biggest attractions is the permanent Nightwish exhibition, opened in 2020 to celebrate the band. Inside sits 30 years’ worth of memorabilia. The exhibition doesn’t just tell the story of the band, it charts Tuomas’s own journey too.

In one room, we spot a photo showing him with neat short hair and a crisp white shirt, looking every inch the nerdy schoolboy. This was before he took a destiny-changing student exchange trip to the US, where he was taken to a Metallica gig. Soon after returning to Finland, he joined local goth/doom band Dismal Silence.

Before our first show, I thought I was going to die

Tuomas Holopainen

“I loved it immediately,” he says. “Being with your mates, playing every night and arranging your own songs. That all happened in the fall of 1993. Ever since, I’ve been in bands: Dismal Silence, then Darkwoods My Betrothed, Nattvindens Gråt and then Nightwish.”

Nattvindens Gråt gave Tuomas his first experience of touring, when they supported Dutch goth-metal band Wish in the summer of 1996.

“We played in Hamburg and there was literally one guy there,” says Tuomas. “He left after two songs. We did 10 shows in 10 days, and the biggest attendance at any of those shows was 70 people.”

Just up the road from the Nightwish exhibition, and directly opposite the baseball stadium, sits the studio where Nightwish recorded their first four albums. It also served as a hangout for Tuomas and his friends, and anyone else who wanted to come along.

“The amount of cigarettes and booze consumed here must be astronomical,” he says.

The studio was also where Nightwish played their first ever show, on New Year’s Eve 1997. Their debut album,

Angels Fall First

, had been released a couple of months earlier and reached No.5 in the Finnish charts. After being offered the chance to go on tour, the band decided to test the water with a hometown show.

“I was so scared I thought I was going to die,” Tuomas admits. “I think I vomited before the show. I’d played shows before, but I was just the keyboardist in those bands, I wasn’t responsible for those songs. Nightwish was my baby, I was like, ‘I can’t fucking do this!’”

As it turned out, they could. Playing for 30 minutes in front of 250 people, the band had a blast.

“We got so drunk that none of us made it home,” Tuomas recalls. “We all slept on the floor side-by-side.”

(Image credit: Press/Nuclear Blast)

In early 1998, the band went out on their first full tour, playing with fellow Finns Children Of Bodom. “We clicked immediately,” Tuomas recalls. “I became friends with Alexi [Laiho, late CoB frontman] right away. Four years later we went to Disneyland Florida with him. We were just two kids who loved the same things – music and Disney theme parks. We were close right up until he died.”

The success of

Angels Fall First

made it clear to Tuomas that it was decision time for Nightwish: they had to dedicate everything to the band or risk it falling apart.

“I spoke to Tarja and Emppu about what ambitions they had,” he recalls. “It was like, ‘Let’s see how this goes for a few years. See how far we can get.’ We got pretty far.”

The band’s second album, 1998’s

Oceanborn

, was another step up. The track

Sacrament Of Wilderness

gave the band their first No.1 single in Finland. Tuomas had taken a job as a supply teacher, and was at work when he found out it had topped the charts.

“I was calling everybody else up to share the news,” he says. “It was up against Madonna and Guns N’ Roses!”

The band got their first No.1 album with 2000’s

Wishmaster

. The same year, they ill-advisedly took part in a competition to become Finland’s entry in the international cheese-fest the Eurovision Song Contest, coming third (“Entirely my idea, everyone else was against it,” concedes Tuomas). More successful was their very first tour of Latin America.

“The response was like we were the Rolling Stones,” Tuomas says. “It felt great to see people going crazy over stuff I’d created in my parents’ house.”

When Tuomas was young, he used to play baseball at Rantakenttä. He still loves the sport, but admits he had to hang up his mitt because he “wasn’t a team player”. When we point out there are at least a couple of people who’ve left Nightwish’s ranks who might agree, he laughs it off.

For all the successes the band have enjoyed, things haven’t always been sunny. In 2001, just as they were picking up serious steam, tensions rose with then-bassist Sami Vänskä to the point where Tuomas seriously considered ending the band altogether.

“Sami’s heart just wasn’t in it anymore,” Tuomas says. “We’re still friends now and there’s no bad blood, but we realised that to stay friends he needed to leave. Then Marko [Hietala, bassist and co-vocalist] joined, of course.”

Four years later, there was even more turbulence. The band’s 2004 album,

Once

, had kicked things to another level for them, not least in the UK and America. But problems were brewing with Tarja Turunen.

“I loved the first half of the Once [Upon A] Tour,” Tuomas says. “Then all hell broke loose in 2005, which was the darkest period of the band.”

He’s referring, of course, to the night of October 21, 2005, when, immediately after the final show of the Once Upon A Tour in Helsinki, the band delivered a letter to Tarja accusing her of putting her solo career above Nightwish and telling her she was fired from the band. After the letter was published online, an ugly media storm broke out. Even the country’s then-Prime Minister was asked to comment on the split in Parliament.

“We get blamed for what happened, for good reason,” says Tuomas. “But there was no future for us together. We were just operating in survival mode and plagued by these dark thoughts. We got completely butchered in the media – it was like we were these evil neanderthals who’d hurt our wonderful ex-singer. I got some really interesting letters, let’s put it that way.”

Tarja and Tuomas have exchanged a few emails in recent years, but Tuomas says that’s as close as they’re likely to get to repairing their relationship.

“It was a divorce, and an ugly one at that, so I think we have our own lives now,” he says. “Someone did say to me if we got Tarja and Marko [Hietala, who left in 2020] back in, we could tour just South America for a year straight. That’s not gonna happen.”

After Tarja’s dismissal, Nightwish found a replacement in Anette Olzon, who joined the band in May 2007. According to Tuomas, she was one of 2,200 candidates who applied for the job.

“We’d already recorded [the music for] the album [2007’s Dark Passion Play], so it was a bit like, ‘The deadline is approaching,’” he says. “None of the 2,200 candidates was immediately spot-on, but Anette was the best of what we had. Her voice was so refreshing to all of us, we loved her interpretations of the songs.”

The split with Tarja didn’t halt Nightwish’s rise.

Dark Passion Play

and 2011’s

Imaginaerum

continued their hot streak, with the latter giving them their first US Top 30 album. Memorably, they played in China for the first time in 2008. Tuomas says the authorities banned them from throwing plectrums into the audience in case fans stood up during the show.

But more upheaval came in 2012 when Anette left the band in controversial circumstances midway through a US tour. She had publicly voiced her displeasure at being temporarily replaced by Arch Enemy’s Alissa White-Gluz and Elize Ryd of Amaranthe at a gig in Denver when she was too ill to perform. Anette subsequently contested that she’d been fired because she was pregnant and could not tour extensively – something the band denied.

Tuomas won’t go into specifics today, but does hint at some regrets about the period.

“It’s so easy to think, ‘We must strike while the iron is hot’, but you have to know your limits,” Tuomas says now. “When Anette joined the band, we started the Dark Passion Play tour, which lasted for two years and 250 shows. We did four American tours on that record alone, just constant touring, and the result is what it was. A silly thing to do.”

John McMurtrie

John McMurtrie

John McMurtrie

John McMurtrie

John McMurtrie

We stop for lunch at a local pizzeria, where we’re greeted by a massive portrait of the band from the Once era. With his long dark hair and gothic clothes, the Tuomas in the painting looks like he’s trying to be Peter Steele.

“Back then I was obsessed with darkness,” he says, looking at the picture with mild embarrassment. “I grew out of it, I’ve changed a lot, personality-wise.”

Certainly, the last decade or so seems to have been more stable for Nightwish, at least when it comes to singers. Former After Forever singer Floor Jansen replaced Anette Olzon as interim vocalist for the remaining dates on the Imaginaerum tour, before joining as a full-time member in 2013.

If we’d continued as we were, people were gonna die

Tuomas Holopainen

The eventual departure of longtime drummer Jukka Nevalainen in 2019 after stepping away from touring five years earlier was amicable (he would ultimately be replaced by Kai Hahto). But Nightwish’s world was rocked once more in the midst of the pandemic, when Marko Hietala dropped a bombshell and announced that he was leaving, citing mental health issues.

“I was gutted,” Tuomas says. “We all knew he’d got his problems with depression. But he called me in December [2020] just saying, ‘I can’t do this anymore. I’m too sick – I need to do something else.’ My initial reaction was laughter – surely it wasn’t happening again. I called Emppu, and he said, ‘Maybe we should quit.’ I agreed.”

However, getting new bassist Jukka Koskinen onboard was a turning point. “Sure enough, everything worked. The sun started to shine again. That’s what this band does: it keeps surviving,” he says, adding that he and Marko are still on good terms.

Even then, the drama wasn’t over. Floor Jansen was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2022 (her treatment was, thankfully, successful). The following year, a shock announcement that the band wouldn’t be touring “for the foreseeable future” set alarm bells ringing among fans.

As we speak, that memorable hometown show at Kitee’s baseball stadium was their last-but-one gig. Reflecting on the decision today, Tuomas insists that it was critical to the band’s survival – he was burned out and concerned about his wellbeing.

“I reached a point where I felt that I couldn’t do it anymore,” he explains. “There’s so much shit that goes on when you’re on tour and I’m slightly traumatised. I told the band they could go on without me, but they wouldn’t have it. Other members of the band said, ‘No, we need a break.’ If we’d continued as we were, people were gonna die.”

Being off the road hasn’t hurt their career. 2024’s

Yesterwynde

continued their chart-topping streak in Finland and gave them their second UK Top 20 album following 2015’s grandiose

Endless Forms Most Beautiful

.

“Nightwish has always been more than the sum of its parts,” Tuomas says bullishly. “I honestly think at this point, if any member – including myself – left, the rest of them could continue. Any of us. Because we have evidence enough that this band can work with any combo.”

Tuomas’s home sits a little way out of Kitee itself. From the outside at least, it exudes a very fitting Addams Family vibe, as well as an air of solitude that seems to suit a man who values his privacy. A jetty juts out on the serene water of a lake. Tuomas often relaxes in his sauna before sitting on the jetty to write lyrics and reflect. He’s had plenty of time to do the latter recently.

“That’s why we’re on a break right now,” he says. “We’ve been in the same job for 30 years – we can take a vacation. I love having the time to read, and take a long walk. But I also don’t want to do that for the rest of my life.”

He’s getting itchy feet. In July, he played a few Finnish shows with Auri, the folk project he formed with his wife, Johanna Kurkela, and Nightwish multi-instrumentalist/ co-vocalist Troy Donockley. Tuomas is also working on his second solo album, with plans to record the final parts later this year. After that, he’s planning to properly start work on the next Nightwish album.

“I got my health back, I feel more inspired than ever – proof of that is that I’ve already got six new Nightwish songs done,” he says. “Every time I sit in front of my keyboard, I’m like, ‘Ah yeah this is great! Just wait till everyone hears this.’ It’s exhilarating. Next year is too early to be going back on tour. The year after, possibly? I want to do another album before any live shows, and that’s definitely happening. We’ve already reserved things for that next year.”

The upcoming

The Greatest 30 Years On Earth

compilation is both proof that rumours of Nightwish’s demise have been greatly exaggerated, and a celebration of the ongoing legacy of the band Tuomas formed in this tiny town all those years ago that has defined his life ever since.

“This stuff will live on for 100 years after I’m dead,” he says. “I wouldn’t have met my wife without Nightwish. It’s brought all the best and worst things into my life, but the good far exceeds the bad.”

The 30 Greatest Years On Earth is out December 11 via Nuclear Blast.

pending_news.title: The story of Pink Floyd's The Wall tour: Power grabs, bad blood, sackings and bitter dysfunction
pending_news.rss_body:
Thanks to a ‘plan’ sketched hastily on a napkin by Nigel Tufnel,

Spinal Tap

’s Stonehenge-themed stage props were famously under-egged, their replica structures a laughable 18 inches high. When

Pink Floyd

toured their 1979 masterpiece

The Wall

, though, the staging and production impressed. Clearly no ‘back of a fag packet’ conception, it involved rigorous input from designer Jonathan Park and architect Mark Fisher. The scale of it all was daunting, vast.

Roger Waters

’ exacting vision required a 33-feet-high, 260-feet-wide barrier/wall to be erected gradually during each show. This was a metaphor, he said, for our psychological defences; for the ultimately problematic shield we put between ourselves and the big bad world. But Waters’ desire to build an actual wall between himself and Floyd’s audience was real and had been seeded years earlier.

Never a huge fan of touring, Waters found his distaste for it grew after the huge success of

The Dark Side Of The Moon

. Gone were the days of playing

Interstellar Overdrive

to the in-crowd in the shadowy, intimate surrounds of London’s UFO Club. Post-Dark Side, Floyd were a household name, playing to massive audiences in huge stadiums. There was no shortage of loons shouting out during the quiet bits, proving that they, too, had ‘always been mad’. Consequently, Waters began to view the gigging experience as analogous to competitive sport; warfare, even.

“It just became more and more oppressive”, he told Sylvie Simmons in 1999. “Those places weren’t built for music. They were built for sporting events, and it’s not unnatural to experience a ritualisation of war, because that’s all sport is. What was going through my mind - my whole body - was an enormous sense of frustration, a feeling of: ‘What are we all doing here? What’s the point?’ The answer that kept clanging back monotonously was: cash and ego. That’s all this is about.”

The audience and stage set for a concert on Pink Floyd's The Wall Tour

(Image credit: Denis O'Regan/Getty Images)

Having first bought a country pile in Horsham in Sussex, then a grander Georgian mansion in the picturesque village of Kimbridge in Hampshire, Waters was no more immune to the trappings of success than his bandmates. Status and wealth didn’t seem to satisfy him, though. Instead he seemed a rather joyless kind of rock star who made an art form of being a curmudgeon.

Waters’ beef with corporate greed and the whole rock’n’roll circus had come to a head at Montreal’s Olympic Stadium on July 6, 1977. It was the final date of Pink Floyd’s Animals In The Flesh tour, and they played to 78,000 people that night. Miffed at a potential stage invader who was screaming at him to play

Careful With That Axe, Eugene

, Waters spat on - or at least at - the overzealous fan. He later re-enacted the moment in fairly graphic detail for Floyd biographer Mark Blake during an interview at London’s Mayfair hotel in 2017.

Was the structure that dominated the stage on The Wall tour designed to keep fans out, then? Or was it to fence Waters’ anger in? Either way, it was a bold piece of theatre that took ingenuity and manpower to construct and knock down.

Still, as dress rehearsals got under way in January 1980 at the MGM film lot in Culver City, Los Angeles there were concerns about the barrier’s efficacy, not least from David Gilmour, whom Waters had charged with putting the band through its paces while he fine-tuned the visuals: “Obviously, when someone says: ‘We’re going to build this fucking great wall across the front of the stage, and we’re going to be playing behind it, and the audience are going to be in front, looking at it’, you go: ‘Hang on a minute - I’m not sure I want to be part of that audience,’” Gilmour recalled.

Gerald Scarfe - the satirist leading the team transforming the cartoons he’d drawn for

The Wall

’s sleeve into giant puppet grotesques and stunning animated projections that would make the live show a multimedia extravaganza – was of the same mind regarding Waters’ on-stage barricade. “Everyone, including [

The Wall

album’s producer] Bob Ezrin said to Roger: ‘You can’t invite the fans into Earls Court and then shut them out,’” Scarfe remembered.

In the end, Waters was persuaded to allow a few peepholes in the gradually materialising wall. That way, perhaps Floyd fans wouldn’t feel as alienated as he did. Through missing bricks, the singer could be spied in a mock-up seedy motel room during

Nobody Home

’s bleak portrayal of an isolated rock star’s drug-addled unravelling. An armchair sourced from West Hollywood’s Tropicana Inn, as frequented by

Jim Morrison

,

Led Zeppelin

and the like, lent the on-stage tableau veracity.

In essence, though, Waters wasn’t for turning, and brokered few compromises. He even ruled out any kind of encore once the wall was toppled during performances of the album’s penultimate song,

The Trial.

He felt

The Wall

album, tour and feature film marked the likely high-water mark of his creative agency and opportunity, so he was determined to do it his way.

“Being a purist, Roger didn’t want a medley of old favourites at the end,” Gerald Scarfe told me in 2009. “I think he saw

The Wall

concerts as being a bit like an opera, a piece that had a clear beginning and a definite end. Encores would have diluted that.”

(Image credit: Alamy )

On

The Wall

, Waters’ cathartic, sometimes emotionally raw songs (witness

Don’t Leave Me Now

) addressed themes even more personal than usual for him. Rooted in his own childhood trauma and feelings of rock-star estrangement, but inhabited by Pink, the concept record’s key protagonist and anti-hero, they had a key tragedy at their core, namely Waters losing his father when he was just five months old.

Eric Fletcher Waters had been a second lieutenant in the Royal Fusiliers, and was killed in Aprilia, Italy in 1944 at the Battle Of Anzio. The resulting pain his son carried with him never diminished. Instead it increased, becoming an all-consuming spur.

Respectful of this truth, but wary of

The Wall

becoming suffocated by it, Bob Ezrin and others around Waters advised him to make its themes more universal. Thus the album grew to explore madness, authoritarianism, substance abuse, lust, paranoia, child-parent bonds and more. Darkly relatable,

The Wall

had axes to grind; causes to get behind; a whole casebook of dents to the psyche. No wonder it went on to sell more than 30 million copies.

Waters’ artistic vision was hugely impressive, then, but participating in it came at a growing cost for his bandmates and other key collaborators. While making the double album that was primarily his baby, Waters snuffed out perceived power grabs and dictated the terms of engagement. He had long since seen himself as Pink Floyd’s de facto leader. And given that he was writing much more material than his bandmates at a time when the group’s tax affairs were such that they really needed to earn, why shouldn’t he?

“Roger’s attitude was: ‘It’s my record and I’ve let the rest of you play on it,’” Bob Ezrin told Blake in

Pigs Might Fly: The Inside Story Of Pink Floyd

. “With everything that was going on financially with the band, he was the one standing there with what he saw as a satchel full of pound notes.”

Roger Waters soaks up the spotlight at Westfalenhalle in Dortmund, Germany, February 1981

(Image credit: Alamy)

Further asserting himself, Waters even dished out badges celebrating the fact that Ezrin would receive a lower royalty rate for his work on

The Wall

than the band. Reading ‘NOPE’, shorthand for No Points Ezrin, these badges were daft, but also slightly cruel, the stuff of schadenfreude.

Ezrin later recalled that Waters’ behaviour reminded him of being bullied at school in his native Toronto. Quite the indictment, given that Waters’ lyric for

The Happiest Days Of Our Lives

railed against his own childhood weaknesses being exposed by bullying teachers. Perhaps

The Wall’

s pain-infused bricks never crumbled. Perhaps they just got passed down the line.

Floyd’s keyboard player Rick Wright also fell foul of Waters’ realpolitik during the making of

The Wall

, and the ramifications for the tour were significant. How Wright came to be sacked by Waters, taking part in the live shows only as a kind of glorified session player, takes unravelling.

Even while making the previous album, 1977’s

Animals

, tensions had arisen between the pair. “Roger started rejecting what I came up with,” Wright told Sylvie Simmons. “It was partly my fault because I didn’t push my material. Or I was too lazy to write anything. My personal life wasn’t happy; my marriage was breaking up.”

By Waters’ account, he and Wright’s relationship soured further as their US record company Columbia’s delivery deadline for

The Wall

pressed. While the band vacationed in August 1979 (separate destinations, natch), Waters asked Floyd manager Steve O’Rourke to contact Wright and impress upon him that it was now imperative that he haste back to LA’s Cherokee Studios to finish his keyboard parts if Floyd were to deliver

The Wall

on time.

Additionally, Columbia were dangling a carrot: Floyd would receive an extra royalty percentage point if they met the deadline. But Wright, now moving towards divorce from his first wife, Juliette Gale, was enjoying rare, sacred time with his kids. To him, Waters’ demand to return to the studio a week early seemed pig-headed.

The Wall at Earls Court in London, 1980

(Image credit: Denis O'Regan/Getty Images)

“[O’Rourke] found Rick in Greece, and Rick’s message was: ‘Tell Roger to fuck off,’” Waters said. “So I gave him an ultimatum to do as he was told and finish the record, keep [his] full share [of the recording royalties] and leave quietly afterwards, or I’d see him in court. He very wisely accepted the former proposal.”

Blake’s book also includes David Gilmour and Nick Mason’s reactions to Wright’s dismissal. These help explain why tensions were running especially high as Pink Floyd completed

The Wall

and began preparing to tour.

“I called [Roger] from a phone box in Chapelizod, just outside Dublin,” Gilmour recalled. “I said: ‘You can’t do that. [Rick’s] been in the band all the way along. If you don’t like it, your choice is to leave. It isn’t to throw someone out… You’re letting this get very personal, aren’t you?’ I won’t quote what Roger said,” Gilmour added, pointedly.

In truth, the guitarist also felt that Wright’s commitment wasn’t what it had been, but he considered the keyboard player’s position in Floyd “sacrosanct”, and clarified his views once they were all back in Los Angeles.

“Rick said: ‘Do you still want me in the band?’ I said, ‘Not particularly, because you’re not doing anything, but I’ll support your right to be in it till the end.’”

“He [Wright] had been forced to hang around, really, not doing anything for months,” Nick Mason told

Prog

’s Daryl Easlea in 2019. “So he had gone stir-crazy and just said: ‘No, I am not giving up my summer holidays.”

Wright also contested the claim that he had told Waters to fuck off. But ultimately, all concerned were outflanked by Waters.

“Roger carried out a brilliant campaign to get what he wanted by a certain amount of cajoling and threatening,” said Mason. “Looking back, I should have stuck up for Rick, but I utterly failed to do so and aligned myself with the forces of safety.”

(Image credit: Rob Verhorst/Redferns)

In May 2022, the Swedish group ABBA’s pioneering, avatar-enabled virtual residency ABBA Voyage opened at London’s Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park. Had the technology been available in 1980, Pink Floyd’s singer and bassist might have utilised it too. “Roger told me he dreamed of having a surrogate band play gigs so he could avoid the tedium of long tours and play golf instead,” Gerald Scarfe recalled. Eighteen holes while the group played on? Even Waters knew this was a pigs-might-fly scenario. Yet his surrogate band fantasy became a reality during key moments of

The Wall

live shows.

Additional musicians and backing vocalists were required to aid the core Floyd quartet bringing the LP’s sometimes complex music to stage. These included guitarist Snowy White, then moonlighting from

Thin Lizzy

, sometime

Status Quo

bassist Andy Bown, plus drummer John ‘Willie’ Wilson and keyboard player Peter Wood, both of whom had played with folk-rock band Sullivan Brothers & Quiver.

Between them, these four wore specially moulded latex masks in the images of Waters, Gilmour, Wright and Mason during concert opener

In The Flesh

. “I had been around Pink Floyd for years,” recalled Wilson, a long-term pal of Gilmour’s, “but it was very weird wearing a mask of Nick Mason’s face.”

Naturally, when the real Pink Floyd appeared it was a coup de théâtre: as

In The Flesh

closed, a model of a Stuka dive bomber crashed into the stage, then the surrogate band froze, the real Floyd stood up, and the crowd realised they’d been hoodwinked. Today, fan-shot YouTube spoilers would have sunk the surrogate set-piece after the opening night, but in 1980 it retained its element of surprise for a little longer.

Nonetheless, some details of the show had been leaked. Bob Ezrin explained how, while he was going through a divorce and fighting for custody of his children, a journalist friend had teased information from him about the performances while he was not at his best, and leaked the story to

Billboard

. The magazine’s spoiler article appeared before the opening night. Consequently, Waters/Ezrin relations were ruined, albeit temporarily.

“Roger went nuclear and had me banned from seeing the show,” the producer recalled. But when the production reached Nassau Coliseum on Long Island, New York in February 24, Ezrin’s cachet there was such that he was able to gain admittance anyway: “I went backstage at the interval, and I think Roger hid in the dressing room.”

David Gilmour on the Wall Tour at Earls Court in London, August 4, 1980

(Image credit: GEMA/IconicPix)

Initially, Pink Floyd played a seven-night run at the Los Angeles Memorial Sports Arena after three weeks of intensive rehearsals.

Surrogate band member Andy Bown recalled: “I remember [Floyd manager] Steve O’Rourke saying: ‘I hope this fucking works, Andy, because we’re two-point-eight million dollars down the pan already.”

“It was the gigantic scale that was so terrifying,” Scarfe remembered. “The whole Roman circus of it. But I just had to generate the ideas - someone else had to work out how things would actually happen technically, architecturally or mechanically.”

Things happening included the 49-foot-high incarnation of Waters’ psychotic Scottish schoolteacher during

Another Brick In The Wall Part 2

, while the 500lb, 35-feet high inflatable mother who arrived during the song of the same name was another grotesque. In Waters and Scarfe’s world, unlike that of a certain

Kate Bush

song, mother did not stand for comfort. Rather, the maternal bond was portrayed as suffocating and controlling, a poisonous thing.

Clearly,

The Wall

live was all risk, a deliberate detonation of normal audience/performer conventions. Or as

Prog

’s Daryl Easlea put it, “a mere 31 [dates] in four cities that fundamentally reshaped the concept of the stadium concert”. Adding to the slap in the face that was the wall’s part obfuscation of the band, Waters arranged for the shows to be introduced by warm-up MCs whose job was to rile the crowd with some creative trolling. Who said prog had learned nothing from punk?

One of these MCs, sometime Saturday Night Live comedian Gary Yudman, recalled the script Waters showed him by way of instruction prior to Floyd’s five-night stand at the Nassau Coliseum: “It said: ‘The MC comes out and talks to the crowd and gets them so pissed off…' Then Roger said to me: ‘I want this, Gary. Can you make them angry? Can you do it?’”

There was tension and bile galore during Floyd’s performances of

The Wall

, but also moments of extraordinary poignancy. For example, who could fail to be moved by Scarfe’s animation sequence for

Goodbye Blue Sky

? Especially as the voices of backing vocalists Jon Joyce, Stan Farber, Jim Haas and Joe Chemay merged in

Beach Boys

-style harmonies as the darkly compelling images played out.

“Whenever I give a talk about my work,” Scarfe said in 2009, “those images I used for

Goodbye Blue Sky

come up. In many ways they explain my childhood experiences of the war as well as Roger’s. Roger and David’s music was incredibly inspiring, because the song is sort of this sad counterpoint to

(There’ll Be Bluebirds Over) The White Cliffs Of Dover. Goodbye Blue Sky

is about the ones that didn’t make it back, who of course included Roger’s father.”

Roger Waters on the Wall Tour at Earls Court in London, August 4, 1980

(Image credit: GEMA/IconicPix)

Talking to journalist Phil Sutcliffe in 1995, Rick Wright aired mixed feelings about

The Wall

tour - although not because he was bitter about being demoted to hired hand.

“We were hidden half the time,” he recalled. “While you were playing, you had lots of roadies running around, putting things up, taking things down. It felt very impersonal.

“I was quite prepared to swallow my pride to go out and play with Dave and Nick,” he added. “Strangely there wasn’t any animosity on stage. I think it’s the nature of my character - I accept what’s happened and make the best of it.”

Elsewhere, when Wright was asked why he agreed to do the tour given Waters’ shenanigans, he responded with admirable honesty. “Maybe I couldn’t handle the idea of just standing up and saying: ‘Right, that’s it. Bye bye.’ I thought if I’m going to leave, at least I know I’ve got another month or so to carry on working - possibly with the hope that things might change.”

Things didn’t change, of course. Waters stuck to his guns, and Gilmour and Mason bent to his will - for now, anyway. But Wright had the last laugh. No longer an official member of Pink Floyd after Waters’ manoeuvring, he wasn’t personally responsible for the hefty financial losses (some $600,000, Waters later said) that The Wall tour incurred. Wright was on $5,000 a show, and recalled “making a little money”.

Meanwhile, Gilmour - very much responsible for the musical, rather than theatrical side of the shows - recalled them being “terrific”, although with some reservations. “I enjoyed them thoroughly, but as they went along I became more aware of the restrictions imposed by something that was so choreographed,” he told Sylvie Simmons.

But there was one piece of choreography that Gilmour wouldn’t have missed for the world. During

Comfortably Numb

, he sang the song’s choruses and delivered its magnificent guitar solo atop the wall. No matter that he was perched precariously on a flight case that his guitar tech Phil Taylor was holding in place on top of a hydraulic lift platform, from the audience’s perspective the guitarist appeared to be floating in mid-air, much more rock god than Humpty Dumpty.

David Gilmour and Roger Waters on 'The Wall' tour at Earls Court, London, August 7, 1980

(Image credit: Pete Still/Redferns)

Gilmour’s elevated platform had a safety rail, which is why Floyd’s road crew dubbed it ‘Dave’s pulpit.’ Dispensing his bluesy benediction, and enjoying crowds and a vantage point not dissimilar to that popes must experience looking out on St. Peter’s Square, Gilmour felt the buzz. “It was a fantastic moment,” he recalled. “Every night there’d be this sort of gasp as the audience looked up and saw me.”

Comfortably Numb

was Gilmour’s chance to shine; the equivalent of that bit in Simon & Garfunkel’s famed free show in NYC’s Central Park where Art Garfunkel steps forward to sing

Bridge Over Troubled Water

, and its writer Paul Simon must play second fiddle.

There were grave tensions between Paul Simon and Art Garfunkel, and there were grave tensions in Floyd. Beneath the surface lay a hotbed of resentment. The band’s middle-class, very English reserve papered over the cracks, but the fissures were there all right, complex and far-reaching, festering away. Waters recalled backstage being “pretty separatist. Separate trailers, none facing each other, with all our little camps. The atmosphere was awful, but the show was so important that I don’t think that affected me at all,” he claimed.

Was that really true, though? If you read that last quote again you can almost smell the cement; almost hear Waters slot another brick of his defensive wall into place. Credit is due, though, regarding Pink Floyd’s frontman’s adherence to one of

The Wall

tour’s key principles.

David Gilmour and Roger Waters, joined by the supporting musicians, as they perform the show's final song, Outside The Wall. Earls Court, London, August 7, 1980

(Image credit: Pete Still/Redferns)

At the end of February 1980, after the Los Angeles and New York dates, promoter Larry Maggid offered Floyd a cool $1 million (four million in today’s money) to stage the show at Philadelphia’s JFK Stadium. The vast space’s capacity was around 102,000 - about 85,000 more than Waters considered desirable or defensible at the time. Waters flatly declined Maggid’s offer, and explained his rationale to his bandmates.

“I said to the others: ‘You’ve all read my explanation of what

The Wall

is about,’” he told journalist Chris Salewicz. “‘It’s three years since we did that last stadium, and I saw then that I would never do one again.

The Wall

was entirely sparked by how awful that was and how I didn’t feel the public or the band got anything out of it that was worthwhile. And that’s why we’ve produced this show for arenas, and I ain’t fucking going.’”

Waters also inferred that his bandmates had considered playing the JFK Stadium show without him: “There was a lot of talk about whether Andy Bown could sing my parts, but in the end they bottled out.”

“I immediately said yes and would have been delighted to do it,” Bown told Mark Blake, seemingly confirming that such a conversation had taken place.

Unsurprisingly, though, Gilmour’s take on Maggid-gate was very different. “Going on tour without Roger never got beyond a band fantasy/joke,” he said. “We never seriously considered doing

The Wall

without Roger.”

All the same, the very idea that touring without Waters was a fantasy his bandmates and supporting cast enjoyed seemed like a dig, Gilmour’s attempt to take Waters down a peg. However you looked at it, the ground was shifting, the power dynamics that governed Floyd’s activities in flux.

By the time Waters, by then solo, performed

The Wall in Berlin in 1990,

moreover, vast crowds no longer seemed to concern him. Still, commemorating the recent historic fall of the actual Berlin Wall, performing where it once stood, in front of an estimated 400,000 people, was a pretty good reason to cut loose and break your own rules. Especially as the concert’s esteemed special guests included

Joni Mitchell

,

Van Morrison

and

Scorpions

.

The crowd lingers in the venue after The Wall concert, Earls Court, August 6, 1980

(Image credit: Rob Verhorst/Redferns)

At the end of February 1980, the original Floyd-performed version of

The Wall

took an extended hiatus after the first 12 dates in Los Angeles and New York. That April,

Run Like Hell

became the last ever Waters/Gilmour co-write to be released as a single, although nobody knew it at the time.

Spring also saw the group return to the UK after a year in various overseas locations as tax exiles. A voluminous shipment of props and state-of-the-art audio-visual tech for

The Wall

tour came with them, as did the show’s 80-strong production crew. It was time for rehearsals at Shepperton film studios to begin for a six-night run at London’s Earls Court.

Rick Wright’s demotion to hired hand had not yet been made public, but in a candid interview with

Newsweek

Waters aired Floyd’s dirty laundry. “We have been pretending we’re all jolly good chaps together, but that hasn’t been true in seven years,” he carped. “I make the decisions. We pretended it was a democracy for a long time, but this album was the big own-up.”

Fortunately, Floyd’s music was still special enough to drown out the white noise of internal bickering. For fans, including future

Prog

writer Daryl Easlea, then 14, the shows at Earls Court that August were mind-blowing, a near religious experience. “I knew my life would never again be the same again,” he wrote some 40 years later.

Just post-punk, Pink Floyd and their latest elaborate concept album were still being pilloried in the press,

The Wall

’s music deemed a snorefest. Unsurprisingly, the record’s attendant live spectacular - the very antithesis of punk’s no-frills music and staging - didn’t get an easy ride either, certainly not from

Melody Maker

.

“If Roger Waters had hung around much longer, I’d have been down the front with a trowel and a bowl of cement, helping the bugger brick himself up,” wrote Allan Jones, reviewing an Earls Court show on August 8. Later in the run, Waters took revenge from the stage, calling Jones “a stupid shit”. No slight against Floyd’s frontman went unnoticed. No battle, it seemed, was too small for him.

As the year played out, Floyd’s four members busied themselves with other projects. Gilmour and his first wife Ginger moved to Hookend Manor in Oxfordshire with their children Alice and Clare. Wright licked his wounds. Mason finished his solo album Nick Mason’s

Fictitious Sports

. Waters turned his attention to the movie version of

The Wall

that would be directed by Alan Parker and released in 1982.

First though, came further live performances of

The Wall

. In February 1981 Floyd played an eight-night run at Westfalenhallen in Dortmund, Germany, then in June a final five-night stand back at Earls Court. The London shows were filmed with a view to using some of the footage in

The Wall

film, but the footage was ultimately deemed unsuitable and canned.

In his afterword for his 2025 book

Pink Floyd Shine On: The Definitive Oral History

, Mark Blake characterises the group’s infighting thus: “If Pink Floyd were a family wedding, Nick Mason would be the toastmaster and the other two would be sat at opposite ends of the top table, complaining about each other to anyone who’ll listen.”

Keyboard player Rick Wright had sadly passed away due to lung cancer in 2008, so the “other two” were of course Waters and Gilmour. Warring stakeholders at the nub of Floyd’s creative flow, the pair somehow made one more Pink Floyd album together. But

The Wall

album and tour’s tensions had shook the band’s foundations, and that album, 1983’s

The Final Cut

, was deeply flawed, and a Waters solo record in all but name. He and Gilmour argued about its political stance. Gilmour thought several songs sub-standard, not good enough to release. Rick Wright didn’t play on the record, and Nick Mason had a restricted role, as much mediator as musician.

“We’d been arguing since 1974, for god’s sake,” Waters told Sylvie Simmons, talking about

The Final Cut

in 1999. “Too long. At a certain point you have to say this is not working, the point has come to break up.”

Waters was the instigator, and shortly after he left Pink Floyd in 1985 he began a legal battle with his former bandmates regarding their continued use of the name Pink Floyd and Pink Floyd material. Once more unto the breach…

Back in June 1981, when the original tour of

The Wall

ended at Earls Court, no one knew that it would be the last time Waters, Gilmour, Wright and Mason would perform on stage together for 24 years. But hell eventually froze over – for one night only. Appearing as

Pink Floyd at the Live 8 benefit in Hyde Park, London

on July 2, 2005, the four men seemed fully aware of the moment’s significance, Waters at times grinning broadly.

For a blissful 23 minutes, walls came tumbling down as they played

Breathe (In The Air), Money, Wish You Were Here, Comfortably Numb

… and no encores, then or since.

With special thanks to Mark Blake for material from his books Pink Floyd: Shine On – The Definitive Oral History, and Pigs Might Fly: The Inside Story Of Pink Floyd. See markrblake.com for details.

pending_news.title: "We can’t get everywhere but we can try!" Iron Maiden announce surprise 2027 North American tour, including headline set at Sonic Temple festival
pending_news.rss_body:
Iron Maiden

have announced a surprise return to North America in 2027, taking in arena shows and festival appearances, including a headline set at the Sonic Temple Art + Music Festival.

Steve Harris says, “As many of our fans know, Maiden were planning on taking a break from live performances in 2027, but we’ve been enjoying this last leg in the USA and Canada so much that we all had a chat and decided we should take the show to parts we missed, particularly the North West and South East. It just seems fair to our many fans there who have given us tremendous support for so many years. We can’t get everywhere but we can try!

"Also, we have always enjoyed playing the many great festivals that are in Europe," he adds, "and wanted to experience a couple more in the USA which we will do at the end of the tour in Columbus [Sonic Temple] and Maryland [Boardwalk Rock]. At festivals you are not just playing to your own fans so it’s always a challenge and we all love a challenge!”

Manager Manager Rod Smallwood adds,

“

The first leg was terrific, huge sell-out crowds of all ages spanning multi-generations, some of the biggest shows we have ever played in North America with rave fan and media reactions, and just a great all round vibe and camaraderie from our fans, including in our Eddie’s Dive Bars everywhere. And I know as I go to every one of them! In fact it was so good we just have to come back and play some places we missed and bring Eddie’s Dive Bars with us!

“It is amazing that even after all these years we played to many more people per show than ever before and headlined our first stadium shows in the USA. We have been selling out arenas in all parts of North America since 1983 - bar a short period in the 90s – and the band’s following here continues to grow despite an almost total lack of mainstream radio support and never even having a track reach the

Billboard

Hot 100! For that we have to thank our amazing fans, and it proves that word of mouth still means a lot. We look forward to seeing you all again next Spring”.

Iron Maiden Run For Your Lives North American Tour 2027

Apr 14: Tacoma Dome, WA

Apr 16: Vancouver Rogers Arena, Canada

Apr 18: Portland Moda Center, OR

Apr 20: Wheatland Toyota Amphitheatre, CA

Apr 22: Chula Vista North Island Credit Union Amphitheatre, CA

Apr 24: San Bernardino Glen Helen Amphitheater, CA

Apr 26: Phoenix Talking Stick Resort Amphitheatre, AZ

Apr 28: Dallas Dos Equis Pavilion, TX

May 01: Tampa Benchmark International Arena, FL

May 02: West Palm Beach iTHINK Financial Amphitheatre, FL

May 05 Atlanta Lakewood Amphitheatre, GA

May 07: Raleigh Coastal Credit Union Music Park at Walnut Creek, NC

May 09: Hartford The Meadows Music Theatre, CT

May 11: Belmont Park UBS Arena, NY

May 14: Sonic Temple, OH

May 16: Boardwalk Rock, MD

Bullet For My Valentine

will support on all arena shows.

Steve Harris

' band will headline Sonic Temple on Friday, May 14. The festival will also feature performances from A Perfect Circle, Primus, Clutch, Sleeping With Sirens, Crowbar, Escape The Fate,

Saosin, and hundreds more acts yet to be announced.

The 2027 weekender is scheduled to take place from May 13 to May 16 at the Historic Crew Stadium in Columbus, Ohio.

PeelingFlesh, Emmure, Showing Teeth, Imminence and Vana have also been announced to play at what has become one of the blue riband events in the global rock and metal calendar.

The full schedule will be announced next week.

Single day passes, weekend passes and VIP packages for 2027's Sonic Temple Art + Music Festival are on-sale now,

here

.

The 2026 edition of Sonic Temple featured My Chemical Romance, Shinedown, Bring Me The Horizon and

Tool

as the headline acts. The sold out event was attended by a record crowd of over 184,000 fans across the weekend.

pending_news.rss_body:
Metallica

have released official footage of the band performing

...And Justice for All

on the opening night of their Life Burns Faster residency at Sphere in Las Vegas.

The nine-minute epic is the title track of

the 1988 album

, the band's fourth LP and their first following the death of bassist

Cliff Burton

a few years earlier.

It was recorded on October 1 and marked the first time they had played the song live in 12 years.

They have also released footage of their performance of

The Call of Ktulu

from the same night.

Both clips can be viewed below.

Metallica are performing 24 dates at the revolutionary Vegas venue, split between October and November of this year and January, February and March of 2027.

Lamb Of God

frontman Randy Blythe has confirmed he has deleted his social media accounts, telling internet trolls "you don't exist."

The vocalist says online criticism of him or his band is no longer a concern since he came off of all major social media platforms.

He only communicates with fans online via his Substack, which requires a paid subscription.

Asked by The Break Down With Nath & Johnny how he feels when people post negative comments online, Blythe says: "They can't, because I deleted my social media.

"Bad news for you guys. You don't exist. I'm not on social media.

"I have a Substack, but only paid subscribers can comment. Beause if you're gonna insult me, you gotta pay me. And then I'm gonna still block you.

"But you're still paying me. Pay me, motherf***er. This is a business."

Meanwhile, Lamb Of God have released pro-shot footage of them performing the track

Blunt Force Blues

during their headline slot at Bloodstock festival in the UK in August.

Metal Hammer's review

of the set says the band's live energy and performance levels "set the bar for live metal" music.

Into Oblivion

earlier this year.
