pending_news.title: Six things you need to know about rising UK doom metal heroes Green Lung
pending_news.rss_body:
For a band still yet to hit their 10-year mark,

Green Lung

have reached heights most of their peers can only dream of. Since forming in 2017 after a “seven-pint deep” conversation in London boozer The Black Heart, and more recently headlining the 3,000-plus capacity Roundhouse at this year’s Desertfest, their anthemic blend of doomy, witchy heavy metal inspired by British folklore, history and mythology has captivated the metal masses.

With each of their albums based on a season, their fourth,

Necropolitan,

represents winter, taking its title from the seven garden cemeteries of Victorian London, from Highgate to Tower Hamlets. We sat down with guitarist Scott Black and vocalist Tom Templar to find out more.

Rural beginnings set them on their path

Growing up in Dorset (Scott) and rural Norfolk (Tom), the pair’s upbringings informed what the band would become.

“I was always a kid who had a lot of obsessions – like bugs and mushrooms and anything weird,” says Templar, who writes Green Lung’s lyrics. “Folklore and mythology were an early obsession of mine. I think it’s because it made the landscape around me have that sense of enchantment.”

“I didn’t grow up in a musical household,” says Black, who writes the music. “Nu metal was big then, and I asked my nan to buy me a

Machine Head

record, and she accidentally bought me

Deep Purple

’s Machine Head – which was very fortuitous for Green Lung.”

Templar is a storyteller at heart

As a child, Templar was always writing stories and making his own music magazines with fictional bands. He now works in book publishing, and Green Lung’s new album

Necropolitan

came from a novel he started as a 21-year-old.

“It was an occult mystery [about London]. But it turns out if you’re 21 years old, and you’ve never been to London, you can’t really write that. But the fun thing is I can now play around with things I’ve written before, and rework them into a Green Lung song.”

Books by other writers also proved inspirational. On

Necropolitan,

the song

Ozymandias

refers to the poem of the same name by British Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley. “That poem really fit the theme of the album,” Templar says. “It’s this meditation on how quickly empires fall and the triumph of nature.”

They want to bring back the art of writing classics

Green Lung aim to write anthems – songs that will be remembered, that audiences can sing along with.

“Iconic songs like

Breaking The Law, Run To The Hills

,” Templar says. “We’re both obsessed with classic songwriting. I feel that honed songcraft is missing from mainstream metal at the moment.”

“I call it ‘propulsive songwriting’,” Black says. “We take the core and musicality of early proto-metal – like

Uriah Heep

,

Rainbow

, Deep Purple, Sabbath – where it was very freeform and experimental, since those guys were inventing it from the ground up, and work on the songcraft.”

For them, heavy metal is spiritual

Many of Green Lung’s lyrics explore spirituality and the occult, but they aren’t practitioners of any particular faith.

Templar: “I was very religious as a kid. But when I was about twelve I renounced Christianity and replaced it with music. I feel like in the last sixty years or so people have flocked to live music as a replacement for a church. There’s so much about heavy metal as a subculture that has similarities to religion: the devotion, the ceremonial gigs, how you dress in a way that identifies you.”

“If you look at the function [organised religion] fulfils,” Scott adds, “like community, identity, that fortification of the self, those are things that metal can be a surrogate for.”

They don’t mind being mocked

When Green Lung played Bloodstock festival in 2024, Templar saw a sign that poked fun at the band’s lyrics.

“It was like: ‘Abandoned Green Lung song titles’,” he says, “with tracks like ‘

Bog Body

’, just a comedy list. The fact they could parody us shows that Green Lung actually means something.”

Their new album symbolises the band’s ethos

Green Lung named

Necropolitan

after seven grand Victorian cemeteries because they represent the power of nature – a subject close to their hearts.

“Each Green Lung album is really about nature and humankind,” Templar says. “These [cemeteries] were monuments for people and are now totally overgrown. There’s this idea that humans are special and will always dominate. Green Lung interrogates that.”

Necropolitan is out now via Nuclear Blast. Green Lung tour Europe in December. For dates and tickets, check the

Green Lung website

.

pending_news.title: Rival Sons' Scott Holiday: The soundtrack of my life
pending_news.rss_body:
Scott Holiday is a child of the desert. A beach dweller these days, the

Rival Sons

guitarist grew up in sight of California’s Mariana mountain range, on the edge of the Mojave riverbed. Summers were spent exploring, taking psychedelics and absorbing otherworldly surroundings. It left clear marks on his musical vocabulary, captured now in his kaleidoscopic debut (under the solo guise of HOL1D4Y)

Topology

. It’s trippy but hooky. Think

Pink Floyd

via

The Beatles

at their weirdest, wrapped in a cinematic package and punctuated by the distinct, suave yet gnarly guitar tones crafted in his day job.

"My stepdad had these massive outdoor speakers, and we would listen to [Pink Floyd’s]

Echoes

while the full Moon came up over the mountains, the stars out," he says. "So when I think of desert music, I think of Pink Floyd and cosmic music.

Topology

fits into that world."

The first music I remember hearing

Some of the first music I took in was on TV shows. The Beatles’ Y

ellow Submarine

I remember pretty deeply – very psychedelic cartoon, comical and light and far-out. And stuff from

Sesame Street

like the

Pinball Number Count

song – you’d be hard-pressed to find a funkier song than that.

The first song I performed live

One of the first things I learned and performed in front of junior high kids was

Rush

’s

Fly By Night

. I think we were playing this song maybe without a singer, so I was covering multiple jobs. Around the same time, I got up with my cousin, who’s a great singer, and we did [Extreme’s]

More Than Words

at my uncle’s wedding – we nailed that one.

The guitar hero

Jeff Beck

. There’s something elusive and visceral and raw and creative and beautiful about Jeff. Also Dave Gilmour, Django Reinhardt, and then you get into the jazz world and it’s Grant Green, Wes Montgomery, Kenny Burrell. Of course, Hendrix and Page. I like modern players too, like Nels Klein, Jonny Greenwood, and Ruban Nielsen from Unknown Mortal Orchestra – nobody ever talks about him.

The singer

If you were gonna force me, I would probably say Aretha Franklin is the ultimate voice, and

David Bowie

the ultimate character-singer voice.

The songwriter

I could get into the Leiber & Stollers, but as a writer, David Bowie,

Bob Dylan

, George, John and Paul, and their individual works.

Joni Mitchell

, Prince…

The greatest album of all time

The first that popped into my head is

The Dark Side Of The Moon

, and in that world I also think of [Hendrix’s]

Axis: Bold As Love, Led Zeppelin IV

. But in hip hop you might pick A Tribe Called Quest’s

Midnight Marauders

, or in the jazz world John Coltrane’s

A Love Supreme

, or

Kind Of Blue

by Miles Davis. And Bob Marley’s

Babylon By Bus

.

The best cover version

Donny Hathaway’s cover of

John Lennon

’s

Jealous Guy

, his 1972 live version. Generally I feel originals are better, but you’d have to be so Lennon-biased to hear those two and go: “The Lennon version’s better.” Donnie’s just feels more realised to the meaning of the song.

The best record I've made

Probably

Topology

, because it’s the only one that is mine [laughs]. With Rival Sons,

Great Western Valkyrie

sticks with me for some weird reason, and I think

Feral Roots

is the other one – we had a certain groove, and a way we were writing that felt really succinct on those two records.

The best live band

Queens Of The Stone Age

. We did a summer with them and they’re hard to beat. Those guys pack a punch. Also

Nine Inch Nails

.

The most underrated band

Spoon, from Austin, Texas. I love that band. I feel like they’ve never made anything bad. When I’m making Rival Sons records or my own, just in the ethic and the quality control, I think of a band like Spoon. They are a benchmark in my head.

Gimme Fiction

is great, but they have no bad records – even their B-side demos.

My Saturday night party song

If I’m on the bus and we’re gonna rev it up, and I’ve got all the crew dudes, I have the ‘Roadie Friday’ playlist. The first song that jumps into my head is Van Halen’s

Dance The Night Away

. And the first five or six Van Halen records, just put them on random – you’re gonna start partying when you hear these songs.

The song that makes mr cry

Keith Richards,

Hate It When You Leave

. There’s something raw with Keith that I just feel like it speaks to me. Keith sings a love song in a way that I feel connected to. Also my partner in Rival Sons [Jay Buchanan]. He wrote a song called

Feel Better

, that’s deep. And I love

Deep Swimming

on his new record.

The song I want played at my funeral

I would want the people I love the most to play things to feel great, and feel love and feel joy. Like The Bar Kays’

Holy Ghost

, which is one of the funkiest songs ever put to tape, and with the message of ‘dance and live until we can’t dance and live any longer’.

Topology is out now via Sacred Tongue/Thirty Tigers.

pending_news.title: From the Delta to Dartford: The 30 greatest British Blues Rock albums ever
pending_news.rss_body:
The British Blues Boom found its fullest expression in late 60s releases from the likes of The Yardbirds,

Cream

and

the Rolling Stones

, when the blues-fuelled energy of the mod clubs in the earlier part of the decade had drifted and all-night dancing had been replaced by a laid-back, dope-smoking vibe.

Key players such as

John Mayall

,

Eric Clapton

and

Peter Green

reached a crossroads in their careers, as the blues scene split between purists and those taking the path towards out-and-out rock. Meanwhile, the likes of Free,

Led Zeppelin

and

Jethro Tull

took their first steps towards 70s greatness, and in doing so inspired a wave of American acts to follow suit.

From Spooky Tooth to Chicken Shack to Ten Years After and beyond, we look back at the British albums and bands that really left their mark.

Frankie Miller - The Rock (Chrysalis, 1975)

Already hailed as one of the finest Scottish soul singers of the 70s, Frankie Miller was dispatched to San Francisco to record his third album with producer Elliot Mazer and a band that included guitarist Henry McCullough and keyboard player Mick Weaver from the Grease Band.

The Rock

’s underlying Stax feel proved what a great singer/songwriter Miller was, with the Memphis Horns kicking (br)ass and the Edwin Hawkins Singers laying down backing vocals on the brilliant

A Fool In Love

.

Ain’t Got No Money

was covered by Bob Seger and Cher, but Miller’s inability to hold on to his band for any period of longevity denied him the success he deserved

Humble Pie - Safe As Yesterday Is (Immediate, 1969)

Formed by Peter Frampton and Steve Marriott in the wake of the Small Faces' demise, Humble Pie were stuffed to the gills with promise that they never fulfilled.

But as their debut album shows, they could rock. Frampton and Marriott bend their guitar strings round each other with passion and sensitivity while bassist Greg Raidley and drummer Jerry Shirley do the same with the rhythm section.

And they took it in turns to add piano or organ overdubs. It’s a masterful blues rock workout. All it lacks is some decent melodies to go with the songs.

Taste - On The Boards (Polydor, 1970)

Unwisely hyped as the new Cream (they even supported them at the farewell Royal Albert Hall shows) just because they were a trio, Taste, featuring a youthful Rory Gallagher, had their own ideas and breathed fresh into the already hackneyed heavy blues scene.

On The Boards

, their second album, adds some jazz influences, particularly when Gallagher plays a saxophone solo on

It’s Happened Before, It’ll Happen Again

. There’s also a folksy tinge to

Railway

And Gun

and

If The Day Was Any Longer

.

But rock is what they do best, as

I’ll Remember

,

Eat My Words

and the opening showstopper

What’s Going On

demonstrate.

Spooky Tooth - Spooky Two (Island, 1969)

It was Spooky Tooth’s misfortune to be sandwiched between Led Zeppelin and Free’s turbo-charged, all-pervasive ascents. A couple of years later, the band’s thoughtful but solid style would have found room to grow.

Keyboard player Gary Wright shares vocals with Mike Harrison, a strong, complementary pair of voices, and also writes most of the songs, including the memorably catchy

Better By You Better Than Me

, later rescued from oblivion by Judas Priest.

The tracks on their second album are an eclectic bunch, blending the blues with folk, country, gospel and even prog. And they sound better now than they did then.

Juicy Lucy - Juicy Lucy (Vertigo, 1969)

Juicy Lucy took their name from a character – a prostitute, in case you were wondering – in

Virgin Soldiers

, Leslie Thomas’s novel about troops serving in the Far East. Formerly a psychedelic combo called The Misunderstood, the Juicy crew struck gold with the first single from their self-titled debut album.

Who Do You Love?

, a crazed hard rock cover of a Bo Diddley song which got to No.14 in the UK, and stayed in the chart for three months.

These days their first album is remembered for another thing entirely: its cover, depicting a naked woman surrounded by fruit. Talk about squeeze my lemon, baby.

Chicken Shack - 40 Blue Fingers Freshly Packed And Ready To Serve (Blue Horizon, 1968)

Whichever way you look at it, Chicken Shack guitarist Stan Webb is chronically under-appreciated. His band is always name-checked as the group that gave the world Fleetwood Mac’s Christine McVie (back when she was Christine Perfect), but Chicken Shack were at the cutting edge of British blues rock.

Stan’s intricate, understated blues lines – heavily influenced by Freddie King – complement his sometimes OTT vocal performance. Just check out his version of King’s

The Letter

on this debut Shack record.

Perfect

gives hints of Mac to come with her laid-back

When The Train

Comes Back

, the perfect antithesis to Webb’s frantic instrumental

Webbed Feet

.

Manfred Mann - The Five Faces Of Manfred Mann (HMV, 1964)

Everyone knows the Manfred Mann hit parade. Less well known is their accomplished take on R&B that was neatly captured on their strangely hit-free debut album.

Keyboard player Manfred, sax/flute/guitar player Mike Vickers and drummer Mike Hugg had a jazz background in common, while singer/harmonica player Paul Jones and guitarist Tom McGuiness hailed from the blues scene.

The resulting fusion is sharp, intelligent and played with style – check out Muddy Waters’

Hoochie Coochie Man

and

Got My Mojo Working

or Howlin Wolf’s

Smokestack Lightning

. They also come up with some sprightly songs of their own like

I’m Your Kingpin

and

Don’t Ask Me What I Say

.

Blind Faith - Blind Faith (Polydor, 1969)

Like Cream’s debut, this (the only) album from Eric Clapton and Ginger Baker’s post-Cream dream-teaming with Steve Winwood was never going to live up to the huge expectations. It’s patchy and inconsistent, certainly.

Alongside a pair of fine Winwood tunes in

Had To Cry Today

and

Can’t Find My Way Home

, there’s a sprightly cover of Buddy Holly’s

Well Alright

and the moody, slow-burning

Sea Of Joy

with Winwood’s soaring vocals bang on the money.

But the everyone-gets-a-solo

Do What You Like

is stretched paper-thin. The highlight is Clapton’s

Presence Of The Lord

, his guitar playing up there with the most spine-tingling in his catalogue.

Graham Bond Organisation - There’s A Bond Between Us (Columbia, 1965)

Before the demons dragged Graham Bond down (and under a tube train in 1974), he piloted a musically inspired but personally fractious band that included Jack Bruce and Ginger Baker, who would of course become two-thirds of Cream.

Catching their uncompromising and expressive brand of R&B in the studio was not easy, and this album is not among producer Robert Stigwood’s finest career achievements. But Bond’s passionate, wailing voice and Hammond are able to cut through the flat production, particularly on

Walking In The Park

. Bruce shows his innovative songwriting credentials with

Hear Me Calling Your Name,

while Baker previews

Toad

on

Camels And Elephants

.

Blodwyn Pig - Ahead Rings Out (Chrysalis, 1969)

The band guitarist Mick Abrahams quit Jethro Tull for after

This Was

, Blodwyn Pig was another quartet, this time pairing Abrahams with sax/flute/fiddle player Jack Lancaster.

But the contrast with Tull couldn’t be greater on their wildly diverse debut. There’s a freewheeling, rocking abandon of

It’s Only Love

and

Sing Me A Song That I Know

, the sweet, gentle

Dear Jill

, the laid-back blues of

Up And Coming

and the heavy metal of

Ain’t Ya Comin’ Home Babe?

The only direct comparison comes on the jazzy, flute-driven

Leave It With Me

, taking over where Ian Anderson left off after

Dharma For One

.

Robin Trower - Bridge Of Sighs (Chrysalis, 1974)

Who would have thought that the “backroom” guitarist with the stately, keyboard-led Procol Harum would become one of the great blues rock guitarists. And it was the second of his power trio’s superb trilogy of back-to-back albums in the mid-70s that sealed his reputation.

From pounding opener,

Day Of The Eagle

, to closer

Little Bit Of Sympathy

, it’s a beautifully balanced, dynamic record filled with quality songs, masterful playing from Trower (

Bridge Of Sighs

,

Too

Rolling Stoned

) with his overdriven, reverb-drenched, swirling psychedelic sound and Hendrix inflexions, plus some outstanding performances (

About To Begin

,

In This Place

) from peerless blues rock vocalist Jimmy Dewar.

Climax Blues Band - Plays On (Parlophone 1969)

These Staffordshire blues terriers sounded a bit too much like John Mayall & The Bluesbreakers on their first album, but the follow-up,

Plays On

, branched out in several directions.

The addition of a mellotron to the mix brings a progressive dimension to the sound, notably on

Mum’s The Word,

based on

Also Sprach Zarathustra

(the

2001

theme). But there’s also Colin Cooper’s jazzy playing on the smoky instrumental

Flight

, the whiff of psychedelia on

Hey

Baby…

and the Latino-tinged

Cubano Chant

.

And there’s still room for some solid blues on

So

Many Roads

and the rip-roaring

Twenty Past Two/Temptation Rag

.

Savoy Brown - Blue Matter (Decca, 1969)

Frequent restructuring blighted Savoy Brown’s career but founder/ guitarist Kim Simmonds got the blend right on their third album,

Blue Matter

, with solid, reliable guitarist “Lonesome” Dave Peverett and Chris Youlden whose distinctive voice was matched by his bowler hat and monocle.

The album is worth it for the slow-building opener,

Train To Nowhere

which is a classic of the era. A simple guitar riff over a bass line sets the scene for Youlden’s soulful vocal, picking up steam with drums and piano before the whistle blows.

Tolling Bells

comes close but sadly Youlden isn’t featured on the live tracks on (what was) side two of the album.

The Groundhogs - Thank Christ For The Bomb (Liberty, 1970)

Breaking out of an increasingly moribund blues scene at the end of the 60s, Tony McPhee swapped his mellow boogie for something heavier and came up with the semi-conceptual

Thank Christ For The Bomb

.

It seemed a risky move, but he had no trouble making the switch. The songs are briefer, but each one packs a punch, even when the emphasis is acoustic. And when the band stretches out on the title track, adding layers of sound after a slow start, McPhee rips out a solo that would not disgrace an MC5 album.

The reward for such bravado was the first of three Top 10 albums.

Rory Gallagher - Tattoo (RCA, 1973)

His mercurial nature makes is hard to choose the definitive Rory Gallagher album, but

Tattoo

comes close, mainly because after four solo albums he’s finally locked in tight with his band.

After grabbing you first by the heart with the evocative, medium-paced

Tattoo’d Lady

and then by the balls with the full-tilt

Cradle Rock

, Gallagher eases back and mixes things up a bit with a blend of Delta blues guitar and jazzy piano on

20⁄20 Vision

or the impressively melodic, languid ballad,

A Million Miles Away

.

But the cornerstone is a pair of stretched-out, rocking blues,

Sleep On A Clothes

Line

and

Who’s That Coming?

Them - Them (Deram, 1965)

Also known as

The Angry Young Them

, the debut album from Belfast’s rabble-rousers begins the way most albums end – with a hell-for-leather jam and the vocals only appearing over a minute into the song.

Van Morrison was contrary right from the start! From the same school as The Rolling Stones, the Morrison-fronted Them covered John Lee Hooker, aped Howlin’ Wolf, and with stonkers like

Gloria

, influenced hell-raising garage bands and pub-rockers everywhere.

If You And I Could Be As Two

, meanwhile, could be the birth of Van’s lost-in-music, high-kicking, piano-shaking, soul man schtick.

John Mayall & The Bluesbreakers - A Hard Road (Decca, 1967)

Replacing Eric Clapton with Peter Green was John Mayall’s masterstroke. While the guitarist stayed less than a year, he left an indelible mark on

A Hard Road

with the instrumental

The SuperNatural

– exploring the sustained tone he’d use for

Albatross

in Fleetwood Mac – and

The Same Way

, which was an embryonic

Man Of The World

.

Mayall had moved on too. There’s an unexpected zest to

Leaping Christine,

and he jousts on bottleneck with Green on Elmore James’

Dust My Broom

.

New drummer Aynsley Dunbar freshens up the rhythm section, but it's Mayall’s blend of original songs and covers that gives the Bluesbreakers their own identity.

Bad Company - Bad Company (Island, 1974)

Bad Company had their fair share of detractors when they burst onto the scene in the mid-70s. Ex-Free men Paul Rodgers (vocals) and Simon Kirke (drums) were criticised for following a more commercial path, despite the fact that their former band had enjoyed several hits.

Completed by Mick Ralphs (guitar, ex-Mott The Hoople) and Boz Burrell (bass, ex-King Crimson and Snafu), Bad Company had Zeppelin’s Peter Grant as their manager – and the American market in their sights.

They struck the bullseye.

Can’t Get Enough

might have had a tasty Top 40 sheen, but it was expertly rendered blues rock to the core.

The Animals - The Animals (Columbia, 1964)

They wrote very little material themselves but the Animals reworked their covers so thoroughly they probably thought they had written them.

So while their debut consists mainly of the standard R&B repertoire – Chuck Berry, Ray Charles, Little Richard – you learn more about the Geordie band’s uninhibited character than many bands who wrote their own songs.

Eric Burdon in particular was prone to personalise any song he fancied and John Lee Hooker’s

I’m

Mad Again

becomes an extended grievance of his own. And

The Story Of Bo Diddley

is a glorious shaggy dog story that incorporates his skewed version of the history of R&B.

Alexis Korner's Blues Incorporated - R&B From The Marquee (Ace Of Clubs, 1962)

Credited as the inspiration behind John Mayall and The Rolling Stones, several of whom played with him, guitarist Alexis Korner began pioneering the blues in the mid-50s, often in tandem with revered harmonica player Cyril Davis.

R&B At The Marquee

qualifies as the first British blues album, drawing on country blues and Chicago electric blues with a particular fondness for Willie Dixon songs.

Blues Incorporated’s approach is unpretentious but still academic compared to the young Turks who would soon consign Korner to yesterday’s man. But without him it’s arguable whether The Stones, Manfred Mann or even the Small Faces would have got started.

Fleetwood Mac - Mr Wonderful (Blue Horizon, 1968)

For many people, Fleetwood Mac’s second album was something of a disappointment after the marvellous debut that established the group as the best British blues band of the day, for which guitarist/ vocalist Peter Green can take most of the credit.

Mr Wonderful

doesn’t have the strength in depth of its predecessor, and guitarist /vocalist Jeremy Spencer’s Elmore James fixation (

Dust My Broom

,

Coming Home…

) was one track away from sinking the ship with an overload of copycat slide playing, but its highlights include some of Mac’s most magical moments.

Shuffle opener

Stop Messin’ Round

is energetic, loose but controlled, featuring some tongue-curling licks from Green – as much fun as you can have with a guitar without getting arrested.

Lazy Poker Blues

is in a similar vein and adds the kind of double-entendre lyrics you might expect from a song title with the word

poker

in it.

Elsewhere,

Need Your

Love Tonight

is an already fine blues ballad given a velvet coating with the surprisingly effective addition of an orchestra.

Love That Burns

highlights Peter Green’s breathtaking playing – one second incisive and biting, the next soft and exquisitely delicate. Completely mesmerising.

Free - Tons Of Sobs (Island, 1968)

Free’s blues heritage is undeniable. Guitarist Paul Kossoff and drummer Simon Kirke came from a blues combo called Black Cat Bones. Vocalist Paul Rodgers arrived from the similar-sounding Brown Sugar, and bassist Andy Fraser had been a Bluesbreaker. Free was a formidable coming together of raw British blues rock talent.

And they didn’t disappoint, coming up with their own distinctive brand of blues on their debut. They didn’t pummel like Zeppelin, caress like Cream or strut like The Rolling Stones. Rather, Free loped and grooved, driven by Kossoff’s aching guitar, Fraser’s throbbing bass and Rodgers’s sonorous voice.

Tons Of Sobs

begins and ends deceptively with the pastoral sounds of

Over The Green Hills (parts one and two)

. But in between there are all-time blues rock classics such as

Worry

,

Walk In My Shadow

and

I’m A Mover

.

Such is their authenticity, these songs sound like they were recorded by crusty old blues legends instead of raw new kids on the block. (Andy Fraser, let us not forget, was barely out of his school uniform at the time of the album recording.)

The standout track on

Tons Of Sobs

is

The Hunter

, a swaggering version of the blues rock staple originally written for Booker T. and the M.G.'s.

Jeff Beck - Truth (Epic, 1968)

By 1968, Jeff Beck had become a major pioneering force on the electric guitar, following Clapton in the Yardbirds, before clocking up two pop hits with

Tallyman

and

Hi-Ho Silver Lining

. By the time he was assembling the band for

Truth

(only later dubbed ‘The Jeff Beck Group’), he determined to make an album for himself.

With Ronnie Wood on bass, Rod Stewart on vocals and guests like Jimmy Page, John Paul Jones and Keith Moon popping up for guest spots on

Beck’s Bolero

, it was an album that not only helped establish the British blues rock sound, but featured many of its best exponents.

Audacious and experimental, it smashes genre conventions at every turn. Willie Dixon’s

You Shook Me

and

I Ain’t Superstitious

are masterfully reinvented, even Broadway hit

Ol’ Man

River

and the Henry VIII-authored

Greensleeves

are dragged into Beck’s musical vision.

Record company execs, meanwhile, thought that Beck was actually Rod: “They said, ‘We always knew that Beck would make it. By the way, who’s the fellow on guitar?’” Beck grimaced later. “They actually said that. I’ve still got those words ringing in my ears.”

Ten Years After - Undead (Deram, 1968)

After the John Mayall/Eric Clapton’s Bluesbreakers album had catapulted producer Mike Vernon into Britain’s premier R&B scout, he spotted the potential of Ten Years After, spearheaded by the guitar pyrotechnics of Alvin Lee.

The band’s self-titled debut album in 1967 was the springboard that enabled them to leap from the UK to America. Suddenly their US record label was demanding a follow-up to maintain the momentum.

Hastily recorded at Klook’s Kleek in West Hampstead, conveniently next door to Decca’s recording studio,

Undead

catches the sweaty, small-club atmosphere and Ten Years After’s free-form approach to the blues with the jazzy, flashy

I May Be Wrong But I Won’t

Be Wrong Always

and

Woodchoppers Ball

, and the moody blues of

Spider In Your Web

.

The encore was a youthful but already potent

I’m Going Home

that would become their defining anthem after it was featured in the

Woodstock

movie. “Basically, that album put it in a nutshell,” says Alvin Lee. “I was so happy with it. When I first heard it, I thought, ‘What are we going to do next?’”

Yardbirds - Five Live Yardbirds (Columbia, 1964)

In the mid-60s, live recording was struggling to reach embryonic status. The technology required had not yet been invented. But the Yardbirds were a hot live band that had failed to capture their vitality in the studio. And London’s Marquee Club, their regular gig, had a recording studio backstage. So they decided to give it a go.

You can get a flavour of the chaos that surrounded the recording of

Five Live Yardbirds

by the frantic, stumbled introductions by compere Hamish Grimes at the beginning of each side of the original album. Mercifully, the Yardbirds were unaffected by the mayhem and delivered their typical high-energy set.

With the exception of Eric Clapton on lead guitar, they were not the most proficient R&B band around. But they more than made up for it with their enthusiasm. And they had a secret weapon: the rave-up, where they sped up into a frenzy that drove the audience wild every time – on Howlin’ Wolf’s

Smokestack Lightning

, the Isley Brothers'

Respectable

and Bo Diddley’s

I’m A Man

and

Here Tis

.

Clapton sets it all up with a blistering

Too Much Monkey

Business,

but

Five Live Yardbirds

is actually a team effort from Keith Relf’s wailing harmonica to Paul Samwell-Smith’s driving bass.

The Jimi Hendrix Experience - Are You Experienced? (Track, 1967)

As Ronnie Wood commented to

Classic Rock

, “It was really Jimi Hendrix who invented that hard rock stuff”.

Electric Ladyland

tends to get all the plaudits but, with

Foxy Lady

,

Manic Depression

,

Red House

,

Fire

and the title track, Hendrix’s first album is like a greatest hits collection, with almost every track an instantly recognisable, timeless rock classic.

It would be nice to say that

Are You Experienced?

set the blueprint for rock as we know it – this was a year before Led Zeppelin, three years before

In Rock

, while Jimi’s tone, riffs and groove make Clapton and Jeff Beck seem like lumbering dinosaurs – but the truth is that few people have even come close to matching the blueprint.

Of the lesser-known tracks,

Remember

would be a straightforward R’n’B crotch-thruster if it wasn’t for Mitchell’s stuttering drumming.

May This Be Love

trips out beautifully,

Third Stone From The Sun

bounds into the psychedelic jungle like a horny panther, while the title track comes on like a four-minute invitation to an orgy to remember.

‘Have

you ever been experienced?’

asks Jimi.

‘I have. Let me prove it to you…’

And then he unleashes a solo that snaps and writhes like a wounded cobra.

Cream - Fresh Cream (Reaction, 1966)

Given the reputations of Eric Clapton, Jack Bruce and Ginger Baker, the feverishly anticipated debut album from this power trio was always going to struggle to live up to expectations. And even though it didn’t, it is still one of the most important albums in 60s blues rock, and its influence on what came afterwards is immense.

Fresh Cream

is a melting pot of ideas, many of which would subsequently be developed and combined with flair and vision to some stunning effect in the following decade.

There’s the colourful, musically informed psychedelic pop of

Dreaming

; the stripped-down, energetic

Rollin’ And Tumblin’

powered along by Bruce’s bluesy wailing vocal and honking harmonica; a bouncy reworking of Robert Johnson’s

Four Until Late

; and six and a half minutes of Willie Dixon’s

Spoonful

on which Cream give a taste of their improvisational skills and Clapton shows flashes of real brilliance.

The real rough diamond, though, is

Sweet Wine

, in which Clapton gradually builds a dense, swirling psychedelic cloud of feedback and sustain that remains as stunning today as it was original then.

Fresh Cream

and

Cream

were the sparks that ignited the blues rock explosion, and without them, who knows how many of rock’s family jewels would not exist today.

Rolling Stones - Rolling Stones No.2 (Decca, 1965)

It was a love of the blues and early American R&B that forged the friendship between a teenage Mick Jagger and Keith Richards down Dartford way, so it’s only fitting that the Rolling Stones’ second release continued to rely upon these building blocks.

Consequently, we’re treated to the fledgling Stones’ take on Chuck Berry’s

You Can’t Catch Me

, a fairly faithful rendering, but with Jagger’s decidedly English sneer and Richards’ rolling, ramshackle riffery adding to its original charm.

The Jagger/Richards songwriting partnership also gains momentum, with three composition credits to their name –

Off The Hook

with its Yardbird-esque guitar motif and relentless refrain;

What A Shame

is a bluesy bruiser and gives bassist Bill Wyman a moment to shine under Brian Jones’s sparse bottleneck, while

Grown Up Wrong

pays real homage to their hero Mr Berry.

But in terms of solid blues prowess, it’s the band’s interpretation of Muddy Waters’

I Can’t Be Satisfied

that truly impresses – Brian Jones’s fluid slide playing on this track was seldom bettered.

No.2

was a monster hit in the UK, and deservedly so, as it convincingly straddled the bridge between the blues and rock’n’roll and set the blueprint for the relentless Rolling Stones march into the future.

Led Zeppelin - Led Zeppelin (Atlantic, 1969)

There’s a great misconception about the first Led Zeppelin album. Many cloth-eared clowns and charlatans regard it as a heavy metal record. How very wrong they are.

Alright, so Robert Plant had the long, tousled hair and the silver-throated scream. Jimmy Page had the raw licks and the feral riffs. And John Bonham had a kit hewn out of solid granite.

But

Zep I

wasn’t metal. It was blues rock at its most epic, awesome and sprawling. It was full of power, passion and pride. It wasn’t just an exercise in vocal and guitar pyrotechnics, with liberal doses of gut-rumbling drum-work on the side.

When this album hit the streets in 1969 it left a crater a mile wide that reached down to Earth’s molten core.

Zep I

was less an isolated collection of tracks and more a searing segue of songs packed with brutal soul and uncompromising emotion.

No one had heard anything like it before… or had they? Zeppelin’s tactic of taking hoary old blues classics and mangling them into fearsome beasts of their own creation came in for fierce criticism. But really, the moans mainly came from blues purists.

After all, when Willie Dixon wrote

I Can’t Quit You Baby

, we’re pretty certain that he had absolutely no idea what he was about to unleash.

John Mayall & The Bluesbreakers With Eric Clapton - Bluesbreakers (Decca 1966)

There isn’t a British blues rock guitarist around whose ears weren’t pinned to the wall the first time they heard

Bluesbreakers

.

John Mayall was already an established player on the British blues scene. Clapton had joined him a year earlier to find purist heaven, first by devouring Mayall’s unrivalled collection of blues albums and then by turning up his guitar and developing the coruscating style that had people scrawling ‘Clapton Is God’ on walls around London.

When the band entered Decca’s West Hampstead studios in April 1966, Clapton set up his gear the same way he did on stage, causing pandemonium in the control room. Producer Mike Vernon and engineer Gus Dudgeon (both of whom would become legendary studio figures) asked him to turn it down, but Clapton refused.

In what proved to be a landmark decision, Vernon and Dudgeon opted to cope with the distortion and adjust the other levels to try and get a balance. What they ended up with was the raw power that can still shock and awe 31 years later. From the opening note of Otis Rush’s

All Your Love

, Clapton’s Gibson Les Paul pierces at mic-shredding volume. After

Bluesbreakers

all British blues albums would be guitar-dominated.

It helps that Clapton is in white-hot form, blazing with the arrogant bravado of youth and self-belief, justifying his ‘God’-like status. After the slow/fast/slow cut and thrust of

All Your Love

he tears into Freddie King’s instrumental

Hideaway

with a mature fluidity and bleeds all over Mayall’s own

Double Crossing Time

with almost reckless abandon.

His vocal debut, on Robert Johnson’s Ramblin’

On My Mind

, is timid compared to his guitar playing, but the song has remained a staple throughout Clapton’s career. And the short, sharp

Steppin’ Out

instrumental was turned into a 15-minute epic in the days of Cream.

But his pièce de résistance comes on the six-minute

Have You Heard

, another Mayall original where Clapton effectively redefines the slow blues guitar solo for the next decade. There are many who will argue that Clapton never played a better, more inspired solo.

Mayall’s contribution to

Bluesbreakers

should not be underestimated. He gives Clapton his head, but he’s still emphatically the band leader and a forceful character, whether he’s singing, playing keyboards or blowing harmonica, which he does on a couple of solo showcase tracks,

Another Man

and

Parchman Farm

.

And then there’s bassist John McVie, paying his dues before Fleetwood Mac and anchoring the rhythm alongside Hughie Flint (still playing in the Blues Band), a lighter drummer than most of his blues rock successors but more than good enough for the job. Producer Vernon believes that Mayall never bettered that album.

“The energy that was created by that band when Eric was with them was special,” he told writer John Pidgeon. “We were lucky. We captured it on that one record. The chemistry was right.”

Bluesbreakers

was the first blues album to chart in the UK, reaching No.6 in the summer of 1966. By then Clapton had already left to form Cream. Things were moving fast.

Want to find your way around John Mayall’s far-reaching back catalogue?

Then try the Buyers Guide.

pending_news.title: Odes to The Old-School: Q&A With Avrak’s Ted Skjellum (Nocturno Culto) and Anders Hegna
pending_news.rss_body:
We recently had the chance to speak with the fine gentlemen behind Norway’s

Avrak

about their self-titled debut album. A devotional work dedicated to the spirit of classic hard rock and heavy metal,

Avrak

bears the character of its two leading lights: scene veteran Anders Hegna and none other than Nocturno Culto himself,

Darkthrone’s

Ted Skjellum.

The project, also featuring Terje Kråbøl on Drums and Steinar Gundersen on bass, gives the listener a fresh, energetic and powerful experience of heavy rock and roll — played by expert craftsmen but still maintaining a spontaneous and unrefined edge. And that’s exactly what the band is going for, as you can tell from our discussion below. It was fascinating to talk to both Ted and Anders about how they got started, how they went about recording the album, and what inspired them along the way. You might be surprised by a couple things, so read on!

(Note: The interview below has been lightly edited for clarity.)

—

Thank you for agreeing to talk with Decibel today! Could you tell me how the project came together?

Anders:

We’ve talked about it a couple of times now, but we’ve known each other for like 10, 12 years or so on a private basis. And so a couple of years ago, we talked about how we should do something together musically. I, of course, knew Ted as a musician and he’s been to some of my concerts. And we just thought that we should try it out and see what happened.

We just filled my car with some musical equipment and went for a kind of a weekend trip up in the mountain. And then we were just like having lots of beers and then we sat down on a Thursday night and kind of connected everything. “And now what? What do we do?” And we just started playing and we had some ideas, both of us. Early on day two, we find out that, yeah, we kind of have something here and it sounded cool.

So we just went from there. So that’s how it started. We didn’t have any plans. We didn’t have any musical directions. We didn’t have anything.

Ted:

So I think one of the slogans we have is that we don’t close any doors. So in this band, so we are up for whatever it is. I mean, we both love the, you know, the eighties heavy metal and metal scene and also the seventies. So we kind of meet on a good level.

I mean, I’m a tiny bit more old school than Anders, but it works out very well because-

Anders:

You’re a tiny bit older as well.

Ted:

A tiny bit. So yeah, but it’s fun because we can kind of combine the ideas and we both learn something new, it’s one of those things that makes doing music interesting. I think it was good to not have a plan on this one, but obviously it’s our love for heavy and hard rock that comes through in this band.

I agree, if you start out with an overcomplicated plan, it could actually stifle your inspiration and make it harder to come up with cool ideas. So with that in mind, for this album, did you have, you know, specific influences in mind? Like a few bands that were like, “Let’s try and like emulate something like that,” or did it all just flow?

Ted:

It was kind of flowing, but the thing is that we have a tradition for now after three years that when we have these gatherings when we actually make music we take some breaks and then we listen to music. It’s almost like a music quiz, like we are just playing classics, you know, from the 60s, 70s, and 80s. I got a problem with the 90s.

I remember when we were going to have the 90s last time and I was, I couldn’t come up with anything, but then I came up with Rob Zombie.

Anders:

Yeah, we tried the 90s, but I guess I have more classics from the 90s.

Ted:

I mean, 90s for me would probably be, since I was a knee deep in the so-called black metal thing, I know a lot of classics when it comes to black metal, but yeah.

Yeah, because you were in your own world during the 90s.

Ted:

Yeah, very much.

When you’re in your own creative space and, to the extent that you were part of a tight-knit scene, you almost don’t realize what’s going on around you.

Ted:

Oh, yeah. I mean, especially I would say up until, I guess, ‘96 or ‘97. I very much was closed in some kind of a bubble. But that was nice, but I did miss a lot of things going on otherwise in the world of music.

Anders:

But just to be sure, if Ted wanted to now create a kind of an old-school black metal thing, he wouldn’t ask me!

So I wasn’t part of that at all. So, but we could have some elements from that part because, okay, I’m 50 years old. I’ve heard a lot of music and I’ve heard things that Ted has done earlier and so on. But this project is just us melting together creatively and trying to make some music that we ourselves think sounds good. That’s just what it is.

Yeah, and that’s all that matters. So do you both kind of share the writing or does one of you do more of music, more of lyrics? How did it kind of shake out for this album?

Ted:

Well, it shook out pretty much 50-50 on everything because we go through every detail together. And if Anders has an idea, we create something out of that. You know, if you heard the album, we have two different arrangement for the guitars almost all the time. We don’t play the same riff together other than, I guess, three, four times on the album. So that’s the way we do it.

And if I have an idea, Anders will do some other things on top of that. And vice versa. So that’s why it takes a bit, it’s a very slow writing process because everything has to work together and sound good, you know?

For what you write, Ted, what would you say makes the writing here different from what you’ve done in the past with

Darkthrone

and other stuff? Because on songs like “Unborn” and “Vard,” I can still hear your

Celtic Frost

influence a little bit, for example.

Ted:

I think, you know, when Anders and I get in the creative bubble, there’s no rules. I mean, we do have, we do come up with ideas. But somebody sent me a review that said the album sounded like heavy metal and hard rock with a black metal undercurrent. I think that’s probably true. And I think there are elements of me, of course, in it as well. I think that was not my plan, basically.

As I said, we didn’t have any plan for how to sound, but I think also the sound production is this kind of dark and ambient.

Anders:

But I think that both of us have our own kind of style of playing guitar. I do a different tuning that Ted does on this album. That’s also part of making it kind of different. But of course you can hear that it’s Ted playing guitar on this because he kind of has his own style. So yeah, I see what you mean.

I think so much of what audiences associate with black metal was shaped by Darkthrone. And so it’s just YOU playing. It sounds like Nocturno Culto. And even if you’re playing something that’s more hard rock, it’s still going to be you.

Ted:

Yeah, that’s the way I play guitar. But for the actual music and for the arrangement and all the melodies and stuff, this has been a very unique experience for me to be working with Anders because, yeah, we spent a lot of time together. I mean, it could have happened on the first night in November of 2023 that it didn’t work.

And I heard you modified yourself Anders because we did that interview earlier and you said we took “some beers” with us, but now we said “a lot of beers” and that’s more correct.

Anders:

Yes, I want to be honest.

Well, the worst that could have happened is you just hung out as a couple of friends, played some music, and drank a lot of beers. That’s still a success!

Ted:

Absolutely!

Anders:

Of course, it could be kind of awkward when two guys are going, “and now we’re going to make music together.” And we had some awkward moments when, for example, when deciding the band name, and that’s not an easy thing to do.

And there was a lot of kind of awkward suggestions on the way. So yeah, it kind of worked out.

Ted:

Yeah, because we understood by the second time we did meet up, we thought that, you know, this is working very well. I mean, the obvious thing we thought about is, well, we have to try to make an album then. So yeah, so we went for that. It took a lot of time, but I think we are happy that we did that because we felt things were going smoothly.

And we needed a drummer because neither of us are drummers, or only if we have to be. And we didn’t want to be drummers. So we got the perfect guy for this album. So he shaped the album because he connected with the music immediately. And so he shaped much of the rhythm of the album and he understood where this was going.

Anders:

He didn’t get any kind of pointers from us, anything. We just sent our two guitar tracks up to him without anything added, how we wanted it to be. So, but when we got the result back from him, we just understood that he was connected to the project.

So, because when I play guitar, I of course have some drums in my head and I have some ideas. And I could say he matched 80% or 90% of my ideas but only better. It was exactly how I figured it was supposed to be. So yeah, couldn’t praise him more. He was just doing an amazing job. And he also spent a lot of time doing it all over and over and over again to make it perfect, he told us. So that’s kind of how we did it as well.

Normally for Avrak, the rehearsal could last for like eight, nine, or 10 hours. And we could play only one song that day. That’s how we did this thing.

So it’s been a lot of grinding.

Ted:

Grinding, yes.

What about the lyrics? You don’t have to go into too much detail, but in general, what would you say the lyrical themes are on this album?

Ted:

Well, I think the cover of the album says a lot about it. We have something to say, but I think good lyrics allow each individual to interpret those lyrics themselves.

But it’s very much about breaking free.

Anders

: It’s a lot of things. I don’t want to label what people are kind of breaking free from. It could be their life and things in their life, in their country or whatever. We try to write lyrics that are kind of universal. It’s not about trying to find the meaning, but trying to say something that people could interpret. So if I find a poem that I like, I want to read the poem and make out the meaning of the poem by myself.

Those are the best poems, when it’s not that obvious what it’s all about.

It should feel like a work of art and not like a pamphlet that someone hands to you.

Anders:

Yeah, I agree.

Ted:

I have to say that for us, this has been one of the absolutely best studio sessions I’ve had in my entire life. I think the studio was a very special and atmospheric place.

And also working with Mr. Valle, Knut Magne, was incredible. I mean, he’s just so professional and a calm guy. I think when I listen to the album now, it’s like being immediately taken back to that kind of atmosphere we had in the studio, which was absolutely awesome.

That’s great. Do you guys have any plans to play live or anything like that?

Ted:

Yeah, we did one show in our local town in April. And, but now with the album out, we are going to have a release concert in Oslo at the Revolver on the 7th of November. And we’re going to play in the Orgium Satanicum festival in Oslo on the 9th of January. And after that, we don’t know. I mean, we are up for playing live. So 2027 will be a good year for us to be taking on those concerts.

Let’s say, younger fans or fans coming from an extreme metal standpoint check out your album and it’s like, “Oh, I wanna hear more stuff like this.” Do either of you have a few classics that you talked about before that you’d wanna list off?

Ted:

Yeah, well, that could be a lot of things. I mean, we did stretch the term “classics” a bit, after a while, but it’s fun. I mean, an obvious classic is “Shot in the Dark” by Ozzy Osbourne, that’s a classic.

Anders:

And if you like two guitars playing different stuff, you could listen to Thin Lizzy, perhaps.

Ted:

Yeah, Thin Lizzy is always a classic.

Ratt is classic for me. I mean, the guitar sound that Ratt had on the

Invasion of Privacy

album is a fantastic heavy metal guitar sound. I love that album.

Anders:

And one thing that I can say that we tried to do on this album is to make the guitar sound the way you would hear it when it comes out of the speaker when you stand in front of it and play. So that’s kind of like when you go out to a music store and try out the guitar and drive some distortion on and play. And that’s how I think that a guitar should sound. So, yeah, that’s kind of a classic way of thinking of the sound, I think.

You can always tell when bands put extra care into the album when you feel like they’re in the room with you playing. Whereas if it’s a little too produced, too modulated, it’s like, it doesn’t sound like a band anymore.

Ted:

Exactly. Exactly the point. I have to add a very important thing that when writing this album, we were sitting together in the same room and creating the music together. But so we also did that in studio.

So when we recorded those guitar tracks, it was together. We played the songs together live on the album. And I like that because then you get this kind of genuine feel that we’re actually playing together.

Anders:

There’s probably some nerds out there saying “Oh, he’s playing that note that isn’t quite perfect” or something. And I’m perfectly happy with that because it’s rock and roll.

We played the songs live and we took two recordings of each song and that’s what’s on the album. But we spent a lot of hours to get to those recordings. So yeah.

Ted:

Yeah, it was fun.

It’s kind of like how they say “Measure 10 times and cut once.” I think it’s key to practice a lot and grind before you record and then record something really great. Because it doesn’t feel the same if you record like tons of takes then smash them all together and kind of make this Frankenstein.

Ted:

I miss that time when bands were recording live more. I mean, rock and roll and metal should be slightly out of control, in my opinion. That makes it so, you know, you can hear that the band actually means what they’re doing.

Anders:

And by the name, it’s a record. So recorded this for five days and that’s what it is. So it’s kind of a timestamp of where we were at that time. We are already starting on some new songs. So for the next album, we’re probably gonna do the same thing and record where we were at that time. So I don’t think we’re going to spend three months in a studio. I would probably kill myself.

Ted:

Oh, that would be horrible.

I actually got a text message from Fenriz today and he said like, I think it was about Black Sabbath. And it said that one of the albums was recorded in 12 hours and he was like really impressed. And that’s nice. I mean, I understand that. Because they recorded the single for “Evil Woman” and the B-side, “Wicked World” in 69’. And the remainder of the album was recorded in a single 12-hour session.

Yeah, there’s a clip that was going around for a while. It’s an interview with Ozzy in the early 80s where he’s talking about how, in the early days of Sabbath, they recorded first album in 12 hours and then Paranoid they recorded in like a week.

But then as they got bigger they kind of just melded into this mentality where they had to go to like exotic locations and take weeks and weeks. And he said by the time you get to Never Say Die, they’re in, they’re freezing in like Toronto at some place that some famous band mixed a live album or whatever. And he was saying what is the point of this? Like, I’m miserable and we’ve been here for weeks and it doesn’t feel like rock and roll anymore.

Ted:

Yeah. Yeah, because it has to be, back to what I said, that it should be slightly out of control. And I think to take your chances and just go for it, you know, I think that’s my way of doing things, I guess. And also with Darkthrone we don’t spend much time in the studio but we are well prepared.

Yeah, you wanna feel like you’re listening to human beings play music. I mean, for certain songs, playing to a click makes sense. But if you start to go beyond there it just starts to lose something.

Ted:

Yes, yes, it can, I know. I’ve been in projects before when some of the album is a bit overcut.

Anders:

I think there’s a minimal editing on this album.

Maybe some things were moved from the take before but just the only the one thing. But everything is still played live.

The production should help you get closer to the sound that you really want, not further away from yourselves.

Ted:

Exactly, and I think, as I always said, the sound production and the sound you’re hearing is supposed to take the listener to your place, you know, whatever place you want it to be. And I always like to compare an album to a painting when you can have a like a really massive, amazing painting in your living room. And that’s the music and the riffs and the production sound is the frame around that picture.

And you can also, of course, slap just a flat plastic frame around your massive, nice painting, but it’s better to have some exotic wood and carve out the details, you know, it takes people to your place.

AVRAK by AVRAK

pending_news.title: The story behind the Foo Fighters' cursed Million Dollar Demos
pending_news.rss_body:
On the weekend of August 18/19, 2001,

Foo Fighters

and

Red Hot Chili Peppers

co-headlined the UK's V festivals, playing to crowds of 50,000 music fans at Weston Park in Staffordshire, and Hylands Park in Chelmsford, Essex. Both bands were flying high on the success of the shows, but on the morning of August 20, Foo Fighters came crashing down to earth, when Dave Grohl was informed that drummer

Taylor Hawkins

had been taken to a London hospital following a drug overdose. The following day, a press statement declared that Hawkins had "overindulged", but was now in a stable condition.

Twenty-five years on, the specifics of the incident referred to within the band as "Taylor's little nap" still remain cloudy. In the 2011 Foo Fighters documentary

Back and Forth,

guitarist Chris Shiflett suggested that Hawkins had taken heroin - "Our soundman at the time was like, '

Taylor fucked up, he's going to die

, he's fucking dead'" - while Hawkins himself blamed an addiction to painkillers, cutting off further queries by saying, "Just fucking painkillers, okay?" Further muddying the waters, Dave Grohl suggested that the drummer was in a coma for "10 or 12 days", while Hawkins insisted it was around 48 hours.

Whatever the truth of the matter, it was sufficiently grave to cause Grohl to briefly consider breaking up the band.

"That was the first time in my life that I ever considered quitting playing music,’ he told me in 2009, "because it had got to the point where I wondered if music just equalled death... I’m in it for the fucking music, but I don’t want to do it if everyone is just going to die all the time."

And yet, by the autumn of 2001, Foo Fighters were back in business, working on a new record, almost as if nothing had happened, as if the trauma of the episode could be managed for all concerned simply by the quartet immersing themselves in music once more.

In an attempt to erase and rewind this troubling chapter of their history, the group attempted to tap back into more innocent, idyllic times, specifically the good vibes of their recording sessions for 1999's

There Is Nothing Left To Lose

at Dave Grohl's home in Virginia. This time around, however, working with producer Adam Kasper and recording engineer Nick Raskulinecz, the quartet struggled to recapture the same degree of creativity. Though Grohl had no shortage of song ideas - at least 20 - constructing fully-formed songs proved taxing, and frustration set in. As the new year dawned, the fruitless Virginia sessions were wound down, and operations shifted back to Los Angeles, specifically to Conway Studios, a state-of-the-art facility on Melrose Avenue.

It had got to the point where I wondered if music just equalled death

Dave Grohl

If Dave Grohl, or his management, imagined that the change of scenery, and the boost given by the LA-based musicians returning to home soil, would serve as a catalyst for inspiration, they were mistaken.

"Nothing was being accomplished," Grohl recalled when we discussed the matter six years later. "The songs lacked any sort of life, they were just weird carbon-copy versions of songs that they were meant to be. It’s hard to explain. And then someone would come in and record half a track and go, 'Okay, I gotta go see my acupuncturist, I’ll be back later'. Meanwhile we’re paying $4,000 a day for this room."

"Honestly what happened is that we started working too soon on the record," he reflected. "We just weren’t ready to do it. We started in on it again before we were ready, before Taylor was ready, before the songs were ready: we felt obligated, in a way. That’s kinda the difference between the first album and the fourth album. In a way they were both made for the same reason – the first album, unconsciously – but the fourth album was a conscious attempt at healing the band. And it didn’t work. It had the opposite effect.’

"We were almost forcing ourselves to make that record," Taylor Hawkins added. "And it just wasn’t right. I just wanted to stay busy... but looking back, I probably could have used three or four months to get my head together."

Relationships within the Foo Fighters camp were hardly improved by Dave Grohl's decision to help out his old friend Josh Homme by playing drums on sessions for the third Queens Of The Stone Age record. Not least because it made Grohl aware that the album he was making with his own band was very much a poor relation by comparison.

"At night I’d go rehearse in a closet with Queens and I’d be in the best band in the world," he admitted. "And then I’d come back to Foo Fighters studio and be totally dismayed by the apathy and lack of any sort of passion. So things started getting tense."

Things came to a head in the spring of 2022, when Foo Fighters invited representatives of the world's biggest music magazines to Conway Studios for advance listens to what they imagined would be their fourth album. While

Kerrang!

writer Ian Winwood was being given a preview of new songs, the long-simmering tensions in the studio exploded.

"I remember getting into a fight in the control room with the

Kerrang!

people outside,’ Grohl recalled. "It wasn’t even a fight, just people making little jabs and little comments here and there. And I said, Okay, do you want me to go and tell those guys that we’re going to break up right fucking now? Because I will. We can if you want.” And then the room was kinda silent."

"I remember getting a promotional schedule for that album, looking at it and thinking, Wait a minute, I don’t even like this music, how am I supposed to promote it? How can I tell anyone I’m proud of this when I’m just not? And to be honest, the last thing in the world the band wanted to do was [for us] to be in the same room as each other."

And so, having already spent around one million dollars on the making of the fourth Foo Fighters album, Dave Grohl took the bold executive decision to take what had been recorded to date and bin it, while he went off to join QOTSA on tour. As much as this put noses out of joint, his bandmates would come to recognise that the time. out saved their band.

"It took about four months to do those Million Dollar Demos, and that’s far too long for a rock record," Taylor Hawkins noted. "Unless you’re doing

A Night at the Opera.

"

In May 2002, with their friendship repaired and heads clear, Dave Grohl and Hawkins would take another stab at the record back in Virginia, and put together an 11-track album in just 13 days. Almost everything the band had recorded in Los Angeles was rearranged, set aside for release as a B-side, or simply discarded, and the duo also wrote new songs -

Low

,

Times Like These

and

Disenchanted Lullaby

among them. Finally, they had a record they considered worthy of release.

Much later, after his band's fourth album,

One By One

, was voted Best Rock Album at the 2004 Grammy Awards, Grohl would confess that, in his opinion, it featured "only four good songs".

"We rushed into it and we rushed out of it,’ he admitted. ‘Too many of the songs on that record just weren’t good enough. It was just a question of getting it done and getting it out... it wasn’t our proudest moment",

By then, however, Foo Fighters were flying high once more, disaster averted.
